question: Which of the following corneal dystrophies is the LEAST common in North America?
explanation: f these choices, Fuchs corneal dystrophy is by far the most common corneal dystrophy followed by lattice, granular, and finally macular dystrophy. Of the three classic stromal dystrophies, macular dystrophy is also the most severe in terms of vision loss. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by mutations in the CHST6 gene (carbohydrate sulfotransferase) on chromosome 16. The symmetric corneal changes of this dystrophy are typically first noticed in the adolescent years as a diffuse, fine, superficial clouding in the central stroma. By the 2nd decade of life, this cloudiness extends to the periphery and typically involves the full thickness of the cornea. The Descemet's membrane may take on a guttate appearance. Macular corneal dystrophy can be associated with severe photophobia and recurrent erosions. There are 3 immunotypes of this dystrophy based on the reactivity of the individual's serum and corneal tissue to an antibody that recognizes sulfated keratan sulfate: • type I: no detectable antigenic keratan sulfate • type IA: serum lacks antigenic keratan sulfate but the keratocytes have antigenic keratan sulfate • type II: normal amounts of antigenic keratan sulfate Histopathologically, macular corneal dystrophy is characterized by the accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) between the stromal lamellae, within the keratocytes and endothelial cells, and underneath the epithelium. These GAGs classically stain with Alcian blue (the mnemonic: "Maryilyn Monroe Always...") but also stain with colloidal iron, Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS), and metachromatic dyes. Of the stromal dystrophies, lattice has the highest rate of recurrence in corneal transplant patients followed by granular and then macular. Of the corneal stromal dystrophies, the age of presentation is the youngest in macular dystrophy followed by lattice and then granular dystrophy.

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy?

options.A: it is a result of a defect in the TGF-beta 2 gene
options.B: Bowman layer is replaced by a sheetlike connective tissue layer on histopathology
options.C: recurrence in penetrating keratoplasty grafts is rare for this disorder
options.D: erosions are less frequent and severe in this dystrophy compared to Thiel- Behnke corneal dystrophy

explanation: In Reis-Buckler corneal dystrophy, Bowman layer is disrupted and/or absent and replaced by a sheetlike connective tissue layer. This is why patients have a lot of epithelial erosions. Only electron microscopy can distinguish Reis-Buckler from Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy (due to the presence of "curly fibers" in Thiel-Behnke). Thiel-Behnke also has Bowman's layer replaced with a fibrocellular material in a pathognomonic "saw-tooth" pattern. Epithelial erosions are typically more frequent and severe with Reis-Bucklers than with Thiel- Behnke. Reis-Bücklers is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is secondary to a mutation in the TGF beta-I gene (not TGF-beta 2). This gene codes for the protein keratoepithelin. Recurence in penetrating keratoplasty grafts is common in Reis-Bucklers.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy?

options.A: it is caused by mutations in the UBIAD1 gene
options.B: electron microscopy of corneas affected by this condition does not show "curly fibers"
options.C: initially, the honeycomb opacities spare the peripheral cornea in this condition
options.D: recurrence in penetrating keratoplasty grafts is rare in this condition

explanation: Thiel-Behnke is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and is caused by mutations in the TGFB1 gene (which codes for keratoepithelin). Like Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy, Thiel- Behnke affects Bowman layer. As an aside, mutations in the UBIAD1 gene are responsible for Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy Thiel-Behnke can only be distinguished from Reis-Bucklers via electron microscopy which shows the presence of "curly fibers" in Thiel-Behnke and does not in Reis-Bucklers. In Thiel-Behnke, Bowman's layer is replaced by a fibrocellular material and forms a "saw- tooth" pattern. Clinically these patients have honeycomb opacities at Bowman level which spare the peripheral cornea. Since the deposits are at the level of Bowman layer, recurrent erosions are common. However, recurrent erosions are typically less frequent and less severe compared to Reis- Buckler.

In Reis-Buckler corneal dystrophy, Bowman layer is disrupted and/or absent and replaced by a sheetlike connective tissue layer. This is why patients have a lot of epithelial erosions. Only electron microscopy can distinguish Reis-Buckler from Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy (due to the presence of "curly fibers" in Thiel-Behnke). Thiel-Behnke also has Bowman's layer replaced with a fibrocellular material in a pathognomonic "saw-tooth" pattern. Epithelial erosions are typically more frequent and severe with Reis-Bucklers than with Thiel- Behnke. Reis-Bücklers is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. It is secondary to a mutation in the TGF beta-I gene (not TGF-beta 2). This gene codes for the protein keratoepithelin. Recurence in penetrating keratoplasty grafts is common in Reis-Bucklers.

question: What is the most common inheritance pattern of posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD or PPMD)?
explanation: Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD or PPMD) is a rare, typically autosomal dominant disorder that is typically asymptomatic. In very rare cases, it can be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. PPCD is characterized by three distinct patterns of posterior corneal findings: (1) a cluster or linear arrangement of vesicles in the posterior cornea surrounded by a gray haze (as seen in the photo below); (2) band lesions; and (3) diffuse opacities. Glaucoma occurs in 10-15% of patients with PPCD. Its phenotype can vary widely with some affected individuals progressing to corneal decompensation, having broad peripheral synechiae, or progressing to advanced glaucoma. Like the iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndromes, it may have iris atrophy, corectopia, and iridocorneal adhesions. Unlike the ICE syndromes which are unilateral, PPMD is bilateral although it can be highly asymmetric. ICE syndromes are also sporadic without any known inheritance pattern. Bottom line: PPMD --> vesicles of posterior cornea + glaucoma in some cases + bilateral + autosomal dominant

question: Q-Posterior amorphous corneal dystrophy is associated with which of the following features?

options.C: increase in the rate of glaucoma

explanation: Posterior amorphous corneal dystrophy (PACD) (not to be confused with PPMD) is characterized by bilateral opacification of the deep stroma associated with central thinning. The patches of "gray-white sheets" affect the cornea diffusely (i.e. from limbus-to-limbus). These lesions can extend to Descemet's membrane and cause posterior bowing. The central cornea can be very thin (e.g. 300 micron range) and flat (e.g. <41 D). Thus, PACD is associated with hyperopia (not myopia). PACD may also be associated with a prominent Schwalbe's line, fine iris processes, iridocorneal adhesions, and corectopia. However, unlike Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, PACD is not associated with an increased rate of glaucoma. PACD occurs during the first decade of life and is very slowly progressive. It typically only has a mild detrimental impact on visual acuity and does not usually require any treatment. PACD is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern; however, no causative gene locus has been identified. The typical differential diagnosis of PACD includes: • Posterior polymorphous dystrophy (PPMD) • pre-Descemet's dystrophy • Congenital hereditary stromal dystrophy (CHSD) • Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) • Interstitial keratitis (IK) • Posterior crocodile shagreen

explanation: The concepts of imbibition pressure (IP) and swelling pressure (SP) are often confusing to students and therefore a review these concepts may be helpful (Figure 1). Normally, the stroma contains negatively-charged glycosaminoglycans (GAGs, mainly dermatan sulfate in the anterior cornea and keratan sulfate in the posterior cornea) which create electrostatic repulsive forces within the stroma. Think of this as an expansive force that is known as the swelling pressure (SP). SP refers to the pressure needed in-vitro to inflate the cornea with a cannula and artificially induce edema and swelling. So a high SP does not mean that the cornea is swollen. Instead, a high SP means that the cornea is resistant to swelling because it has formidable cohesiveness and tensile stiffness (elasticity) that resists expansion. This has been measured around +55 mm Hg. If the stroma is compressed (eg, high IOP, mechanical applanation), then the SP will increase as well. However, if the stroma is expanded (eg, corneal edema), then SP will decrease. The major forces that influence the flow of aqueous into and out of the cornea can be summarized by IP = IOP - SP (where IP is imbibition pressure, IOP is intraocular pressure, and SP is swelling pressure). IP is basically a measurement of the propensity of the cornea to develop edema. As a basic rule, we want IP to be low and ideally negative, because if the IP value increases, then there is likely corneal edema. In vitro, IP = SP (because there's no IOP present, duh!). In vivo, SP is higher than IOP due to the reasons mentioned in the previous paragraph. So usually, IP = IOP - SP ==> 15mm Hg - 55 mm Hg = -40 mg Hg. When IP is negative, then there is no net flow of aqueous into the cornea. However, in pathological states, IP may become positive (ie, either IOP can increase or SP can decrease) and aqueous will enter the cornea edema will ensue. Disruptions to the endothelium (eg, Fuchs) will compromise the integrity of the stroma and will lower the SP value --> increase in IP --> edema. For the sake of completeness, conditions that elevate the IOP (eg, angle closure glaucoma) will then increase the IP as well. Lowering the IOP with topical medications (Choice C) in patients with compromised endothelium can then subsequently reduce the IP. It is noteworthy that the mechanism for hypertonic sodium chloride (Muro 128) is different in that it helps to increase SP which leads to reduced IP. Hence, using both of these medications in synergy may be especially helpful for medical management of corneal edema. While a full review of Fuch's endothelial dystrophy may be found in the explanations to other questions on this website, suffice it to say that vision in these patients is worse in the morning (choice A) and guttae appear centrally at first (choice B). Finally, the new standard for transplants in Fuchs Dystrophy is no longer a full-thickness penetrating keratoplasty (choice D), but rather a partial posterior corneal transplant: either Descemet Stripping Automated Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSAEK) or Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty (DMEK).

options.D: LASEK is a good option for anterior stromal haze in this condition

explanation: Avellino corneal dystrophy (ACD) has been reclassified as Granular corneal dystrophy type 2 (GCD2). It can be thought of as a combination of lattice and granular corneal dystrophies. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and is due to a defect in the 5q31 locus (not 7q31) which contains the TGFB1 gene (which itself encodes the keratoepithelin protein). The corneal opacities are described as looking like: stellate (star-like), snowflake, and icicle (see photo). Lattice lines are seen deep to these. Because the deposits in ACD have both lattice and granular-type components, these deposits stain with both Congo Red and Masson Trichrome. The granular-like deposits have a snowflake- like appearance and are located in the anterior to mid-stroma. The lattice lines are located in the deeper stroma. LASIK and LASEK are contraindicated with Avellino dystrophy because they can make the haze worse. Epi-LASIK involves using a blunt microkeratome to remove only the epithelium and then ablating the stromal bed. The plane of separation is between the basement membrane and Bowman's layer. Early reports recommended replacing the cleaved epithelium, but most clinicians abandoned this practice as a benefit was not shown. LASEK involves placing alcohol on the epithelium and then removing the epithelium, lasering the bed, and then placing the epithelium back on the bed. Again, most clinicians have abandoned puting the epithelium back on as a benefit has not been shown. In LASEK, the epithelial basement membrane is cleaved in half between the lamina lucida and lamina densa. Some studies suggested that leaving behind the lamina densa actually gave an improved post-operative refractive result compared to epi-LASIK. These studies combined with a $40,000 price tag for the keratome was a death sentence for the epi-LASIK procedure. PRK (photorefractive keratectomy) involves scraping the epithelium off with a brush or spatula and then ablating the stromal bed.

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of congenital stromal corneal dystrophy (CSCD)?

explanation: CSCD is a very rare disorder that presents at birth. It is a non-progressive disease (i.e. does not get worse with age). It features bilateral opacification of the central stroma (primarily in the anterior stroma, but can occur at all levels) with whitish flakes. The peripheral cornea is clear. The central opacities result in moderate-to-severe visual loss. The epithelium is intact and erosions, edema, or decreased corneal sensation do not occur. No stromal edema occurs and the endothelium is normal in CSCD which are in contrast to congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED). CSCD is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the decorin gene (chromosome 12).

question: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation to the cornea in the form of welding burns or snow blindness is the result of damage to which layer of the cornea?

question: Which of the following is a TRUE statement regarding chemical injuries?

options.A: Corneal acid chemical injuries rapidly degrade the proteoglycans of the cornea.
options.B: Corneal acid chemical injuries are more likely to result in vision loss.
options.C: Corneal alkali chemical injuries more commonly lead to glaucoma than corneal acid chemical injuries.
options.D: Bases are more likely than acids to precipitate corneal proteins.

explanation: Actually, acidic chemicals denature and precipitate proteins in the tissues they contact. These precipitated proteins then serve as a type of barrier to further damage by the acidic chemical. In addition, ocular tissues have a higher buffering capacity for acidic compounds. In contrast, alkali chemicals cause saponification of fatty acids in cell membranes (e.g. corneal epithelium) which leads to cellular disruption. After the corneal epithelium is destroyed, the alkali chemical can easily penetrate and destroy the collagen fibrils and proteoglycans in the corneal stroma. In addition, very strong alkali chemicals can eat through the cornea and enter the anterior chamber with disastrous results, including a high incidence of severe glaucoma. The most important step for chemical injuries of any kind is immediate and copious irrigation with water or balanced saline solution. Do NOT try to neutralize a base with an acid or vice versa.

question: Which of the following treatments is generally LEAST preferred for the condition seen in the image?

options.A: remove intraocular silicone oil if safe

explanation: This is a picture of band keratopathy, a corneal degeneration wherein calcium is deposited into subepithelial layers (primarily epithelial basement membrane, Bowman's layer and anterior stroma). Deposits may initially be relatively translucent (non light- blocking), but may progress into opaque (light-blocking) entities that may then cause elevations in the overlying epithelial surface, leading to chronic irritation and epitheliopathy. The causes of band keratopathy are many, and can be divided into "C" categories to help make it easier to remember: 1) Chronic eye disease: uveitis, long-standing retinal detachment, late sequelae of HSV infection, chronic corneal graft rejection, phthisis, exposure keratopathy, etc. 2) Causes of increased calcium levels [choice B] (eg, sarcoidosis, hyperparathyroidism, multiple myeloma, etc). Note there is conflicting evidence in the literature regarding low or high phosphate levels contributing to band keratopathy. 3) Chemical exposure: intraocular silicone oil (choice A), thiazides, mercury, phosphate- containing drops (eg, prednisolone phosphate [not the more commonly used prednisolone acetate]) 4) Congenital causes: congenital eye diseases, such as congenital band keratopathy, Norrie's disease, etc. For mild cases of band keratopathy, treatment primarily involves lubrication of the ocular surface and other comfort measures such as a bandage contact lens. If there are treatable systemic causes of elevated calcium, these should be treated as well and may require co-management with an internist, nephrologist, etc. For advanced, symptomatic cases of band keratopathy, surgical intervention may be required. This includes: a) Manual epithelial debridement (superficial keratectomy) and removal of calcium deposits, with or without 2-5% EDTA (*) as a chelating agent, and with or without diamond-burr polishing of underlying Bowman's membrane. b) Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK): PTK is generally not recommended because the calcium will ablate at a slower rate than the corneal stroma and the patient will wind up with irregular astigmatism. Under desperate circumstances, PTK can be tried after all other therapies have failed. *Clinically relevant note: This may sound obvious, but if you perform a chelation, you must make sure that you do not simply order "EDTA" because the pharmacy may send you CALCIUM EDTA (a more readily available substance), which would be completely useless to remove calcium! You must make sure to order either sodium EDTA or potassium EDTA. Extra: Disease Band Keratopathy is a corneal degeneration that is most often composed of fine dust-like calcium deposits in the sub-epithelium, Bowman’s layer and the anterior stroma. It is typically a band-shaped, horizontal opacity that grows from the peripheral cornea towards the central cornea. Initial deposits are gray but as the deposition progresses, the band becomes chalky- white and with dots in areas of corneal nerves. Band keratopathy can be caused by systemic causes (autoimmune, renal disease), as a result of introacular surgery or chronic intraocular conditions, or be idiopathic. Physical examination Physical exam findings in band keratopathy includes decreased visual acuity (often mild) with characteristic slit lamp exam findings: • Gray-white plaque with fine, dusty deposits in a horizontal band distribution on the cornea • Sparing of the extreme periphery of the cornea (normal lucency) • Lucent holes in plaque (representing corneal nerves through Bowman’s membrane) • Flakey, peripheral plaque

question: Which of the following conditions can cause the corneal finding seen in the photo above?
explanation: The slit-lamp photo depicts the classic appearance of band keratopathy. There is deposition of calcium mainly in Bowman layer but also some in the anterior stroma. Common causes of band keratopathy include: uveitis, elevated phosphorous level (e.g. in renal failure patients), elevated calcium level (e.g. sarcoidosis, hyperparathyroidism), and decreased potassium level can predispose to this condition. Also, silicone oil instillation (especially in an aphakic eye) commonly can cause band keratopathy. An unusual cause of band keratopathy is exposure to Mercurial vapors. These calcium deposits can be removed by: (1) First, removing the corneal epithelium (e.g. with alcohol); (2) Applying disodium EDTA to loosen the calcium deposits; and (3) gently removing the deposits by rubbing with Weck-Cel sponges. Some astute OQ users have noted that primary hyperparathyroidism has high calcium levels and low phosphorous levels. Therefore, they believe that answer choice B could be correct. However, it is not the low level of phosphate that is associated with band keratopathy as the question asks. It is the high level of calcium associated with hyperparathyroidism that causes band keratopathy.

question: In addition to calcium, what other substance may deposit in the anterior cornea to cause clinical signs and symptoms of band keratopathy?
explanation: Band keratopathy occurs in "calcific" and "noncalcific" forms. Either entity is caused by a deposition of substances at the level of Bowman's layer. Classic "calcific" band keratopathy refers to the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite and has a multitude of causes including: • Hypercalcemia (e.g. hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D toxicity, milk- alkali syndrome). • Chronic ocular disease (e.g. juvenile idiopathic arthritis, interstitial keratitis, phthisis bulbi). • Primary hereditary band keratopathy. • Hyper- and hypo- phosphatasia (e.g. in chronic renal failure patients). • Chronic exposure to mercurial vapors or mercurial preservatives (e.g. in some eyedrops). • silicone oil in aphakic eye. In addition to the classic form of calcific band keratopathy, a similar form of band keratopathy may result from the deposition of urates in the cornea. These deposits are usually brown (compared to the gray-white deposits of calcific band keratopathy) and are often secondary to systemic conditions such as gout or hyperuricemia. Another example of non-calcific band keratopathy occurs in advanced forms of spheroidal degeneration. Classic calcific band keratopathy typically beings at the corneal peripheral at the 3 and 9 o'clock meridians. Typically, this early peripheral form is demarcated from the limbus by a clear zone which is thought to be caused by the buffering capacity of the limbal vessels. Calcific band keratopathy typically begins gray in color but later turns chalky white. If a patient presents with band keratopathy of unknown etiology (e.g. no known chronic ocular inflammation), then a systemic workup should be initiated. An example of a workup for possible systemic causes includes: • serum calcium, phosphorus, uric acid • blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine (Cr) • parathyroid hormone • angiotensin-converting enzyme • urinanalysis If an underlying systemic condition (e.g. hypercalcemia) is found, then it should be treated to help limit the magnitude of band keratopathy. However oftentimes, only incomplete regression of the band keratopathy is achieved. For patients with more advanced forms of band keratopathy affecting their vision or causing ocular discomfort (e.g. photophobia, tearing), then superficial keratectomy using EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) can be employed. The typical protocol involves: 1. Topical anesthetic 2. Scrapping off the corneal epithelium (since EDTA cannot penetrate intact epithelium) 3. Soaking the areas of band keratopathy with EDTA (e.g. 1%) with saturated cellulose sponges. 4. Scrapping off the areas of band keratopathy with a blade. 5. Using a diamond burr to polish the corneal surface to ensure that it is smooth. 6. Apply a bandage contact lens (with or without amniotic membrane) to help with epithelial regrowh, prevention of haze, and improve patient comfort. 7. Topical antibiotic and steroid drops. Summary: band keratopathy is typically caused by calcium hydroxyapatite deposits but can also be caused by deposition of urate.

question: Which of the following topical medications is associated with dark deposits in the conjunctiva:
explanation: Epinephrine was a glaucoma eyedrop that was formerly used in the United States. It is no longer commercially available. Its use is associated with significant systemic and ocular side effects which include headache, palpitations, and arrhythmias. The unique ocular side effect associated with epinephrine is the formation of black deposits in the conjunctiva (see photo below). These deposits represent oxidation reactions of epinephrine. Another ocular side effect of topical epinephrine is a cystoid maculopathy that can occur if used in aphakic patients.

question: A patient presents to your clinic and states that he was struck in the eye two months ago. He went to the emergency room and they told him that he had a lot of blood inside of his eye. You examine him and note the following findings (see photo). What is the pattern of clearance from the cornea in this condition?
explanation: This is a picture of corneal blood staining. After blood staining occurs, the cornea will clear from the periphery first, then to the center of the cornea (i.e. centripetally). Corneal blood staining is one of the most feared complications that occurs after hyphema, especially in the setting of rebleeding. Approximately <5% of patients after traumatic hyphema develop rebleeding which occurs most frequently between 2 and 5 days after the initial injury. Of those individuals that rebleed, approximately half of them will develop elevated intraocular pressure which predisposes the eye to corneal blood staining. The mechanism of blood staining is that the red blood cells in the anterior chamber release hemoglobin which penetrates the posterior corneal stroma. The keratocytes then absorb the hemoglobin and convert it into hemosiderin which leads to keratocyte death. The reason that corneal blood staining is important is because it can lead to loss of corneal transparency for years and can lead to the development of amblyopia in young children. Extra: CentriFuge, Flee from center. he cornea will clear from the periphery first, then to the center of the cornea (i.e. centripetally). Disease Corneal blood staining typically occurs after significant and prolonged hyphema, usually the result of ocular trauma, and especially in cases of chronically elevated intraocular pressure. The opacification consists of hemosiderin that has become embedded in the corneal stroma. It can take months, if not years for the cornea to clear, but with patience, it can clear completely. Unfortunately, the periphery clears first followed by the center.

question: After how many days does rebleeding generally occur after a traumatic hyphema?
explanation: "Rebleeding" is the major worry after a traumatic hyphema since it can lead to corneal blood staining, poorly-controlled glaucoma, and subsequent optic atrophy. Many studies have shown rebleeding to be a major risk factor in poor visual outcome after traumatic hyphema. Per the BCSC Cornea, it generally occurs 2 to 5 days after the initial hyphema when the original clot retracts. Per the BCSC Glaucoma, it generally occurs 3-7 days after the initial hyphema.

question: You are given the following photo and told that it developed without trauma in a 60 year old adult with diabetes who had a history of uncomplicated cataract surgery 10 years ago. He has not had this condition before. What is the LEAST LIKELY cause of this condition?
explanation: This is a spontaneous hyphema in an adult. Xanthogranuloma (JXG) almost always presents initially in children. JXG is a type of non-Langerhan's cell histiocytosis; histopathology of a skin lesion would show Touton giant cells and large foamy histiocytes. These patients frequently present before the age of 1 year. The iris lesions are not malignant but may cause spontaneous hyphemas. Extra:

question: How do you distinguish recurrent erosions secondary to a previous history of trauma versus ones that are caused by anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD)?

options.A: Obtain an anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT)
options.B: Look for subtle anterior lenticular changes
options.C: Obtain a specular microscopy of the involved eye

explanation: The most common causes of recurrent erosion syndrome is from anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD) and secondary to trauma. To distinguish pottraumatic erosion from dystrophic erosion, the examiner should examine the fellow eye after maximal pupillary dilation. It is much easier to detect subtle ABMD changes after the pupil is dilated since the characteristic fingerprints and whorls can be better seen in retroillumination. If no ABMD changes are found, then the most likely cause of the erosions is from previous trauma. ABMD is the most common corneal dystrophy with approximately 6-18% of the population being affected. It is more frequently detected in individuals over the age of 50 years. The characteristic corneal findings found on slit-lamp exam are: fingerprint lines, dots/microcysts; map lines; and bleb/cobblestone pattern. Approximately 10% of patients with ABMD will experience recurrent erosions. Conversely, approximately 50% of patients with recurrent erosions will have ABMD. It typically has a sporadic inheritance, but some cases may follow an autosomal dominant pattern (with incomplete penetrance).

question: Which of the following would be the first-line treatment for recurrent erosions secondary to anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD)?
explanation: Patients with ABMD (aka "map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy") are predisposed to recurrent erosions due to poor adhesion of the epithelium to the underlying basement membrane. Conservative therapy to prevent recurrent erosions consists of hypertonic saline eyedrops and/or bandage contact lens use. Epithelial debridement is a better treatment for epithelial erosions secondary to basement membrane dystrophy. If these fail to prevent the erosions, then more invasive therapy is indicated such as anterior stromal micropuncture or PTK. Recurrent erosions secondary to shearing injuries (e.g. fingernail to the eye) are more amenable to "anterior stromal micropuncture." This procedure consists of using a specially-designed 25-gauge needle and making many superficial puncture wounds in the involved area. These puncture sites are thought to stimulate adhesion of the epithelium to the basement membrane. Care should be exercised in performing this procedure in the visual axis as this procedure can sometimes lead to scarring. Extra:

question: Which of the following is most suggestive of congenital glaucoma in a 1-year-old?
explanation: Congenital glaucoma is associated with photophobia, corneal edema, corneal diameter greater than 12 mm, and horizontal tears in Descemet's membrane. These horizontal corneal irregularities are also known as Haab striae. Vertical tears in Descemet's membrane are associated with birth trauma with forceps delivery. Congenital glaucoma displays the triad of photophobia, tearing, and blepharospasm with bright lights. In addition, horizontal diameters are abnormally increased (normal for newborns: 9.5-10.5 mm). The first gene demonstrated to be involved in congenital glaucoma was CYP1B1 which encodes a protein in the cytochrome P450 enzyme family. Though corneal edema can occur in patients with congenital glaucoma, it is not part of the classic triad. From one of our users: Haab's striae - "H"orizontal Traumatic forceps-assisted Vaginal delivery - Vertical Vogt's striae - "V"ertical (can be rarely horizontal; are stress lines)

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding possible corneal findings associated with birth trauma?

options.A: the tears in Descemet's membrane are typically concentric to the limbus
options.B: right eyes are more affected than left eyes
options.C: the tears in Descemet's membrane typically occur bilaterally
options.D: left eyes are more affected than right eyes

explanation: The cornea of a newborn may be injured from placement of the forceps across the globe/orbit during delivery. This causes compression of the globe vertically which stretches the cornea horizontally. This results in a vertical pattern of Descemet's tears. An easy way to remember this is that birth involves the Vagina --> Vertical tears. Left eyes are more commonly affected than right eyes due to the way that most newborns present in the birth canal (i.e. left-occiput-anterior position). Most cases of Descemet's tears due to birth trauma are unilateral.

question: In what layer of the cornea is hyaline material deposited in Salzmann nodular degeneration?
explanation: Salzmann nodular degeneration is a type of nonspecific avascular subepithelial fibrosis with hyaline and basement membrane material deposited in Bowman's layer. This degeneration can occur from chronic keratitis and some causes include phlyctenulosis, trachoma, and interstitial keratitis. It is more common in middle- age and older women. Treatment consists of lubrication and, if severe, removing the nodules (e.g. via scraping with a blade). Extra: Salzman=bowman Figure 2. Fluorescein stain highlights discrete nodules within the cornea.[3] Figure 1. A nodule of hyalinized material can be seen causing an elevation of the attenuated corneal epithelium that is overlying it. A defect in Bowman’s layer can also be seen toward the periphery of the nodule (right side).[9] Disease Entity Salzmann’s nodular degeneration SND is a slowly progressive condition in which gray-white to bluish nodules measuring 1-3 mm are seen anterior to Bowman’s layer of the cornea, usually bilaterally[1],[2],[3]. These elevated nodules can be located near the limbus or in the mid- peripheral cornea Risk Factors Meibomian gland dysfunction is the most common coexistent condition[7]. SND has been shown to co-occur in patients with a history of ocular surface disease, including phlyctenulosis, vernal keratoconjunctivitis, interstitial keratitis, trachoma, scarlet fever, measles, and other viral diseases[4]. SND can also occur in patients with chronically dry eyes, chronic blepharitis, trichiasis, previous ocular trauma, and post-operatively (including after cataract removal Diagnosis The diagnosis of SND is usually made clinically. Slit lamp exam can show grey-white to bluish nodules posterior to the corneal epithelium[9]. These nodules can occasionally stain with fluorescein (figure 2)[3]. Corneal topography can reveal significant irregular astigmatism occurring as a result of Salzmann nodules

question: What is the pathophysiology underlying the corneal pigmentation indicated by the arrow?

options.D: Iron deposition following prior metal grinding injury

explanation: The brown pigmentation located centrally in this cornea and indicated by the white arrow represents a type of iron line seen in about 80% of patients with prior radial keratotomy. "Iron lines" form from epithelial iron deposition in areas with pooling of tears related to corneal surface irregularities. This particular iron line is sometimes referred to as a "tear star" because it can take on a star or asterix like appearance (not as evident in this photo). Iron lines are generally NOT visually significant. Additional well known corneal iron lines include "Ferry's line" at the leading edge of a filtering bleb, "Fleisher ring or line" surrounding the base of a cone in keratoconus, "Stocker's line" at the leading edge of a pterygium, and "Hudson- Stahli line" at the upper border of the normal tear layer (commonly seen in elderly individuals). Elevated serum copper levels may occur in Wilson disease. Late in the disease course patients develop a peripheral corneal Kayser-Fleischer ring at the level of Descemet's membrane. Chronic epinephrine drop utilization can cause "adrenochrome" deposits in the conjunctiva. These deposits have little clinical significance but is a popular exam topic. Iron deposition can occur in the form of a "rust ring" following metal foreign body injuries to the cornea. Such an injury would be expected to form a ring, may leave a corneal scar, and would not be associated with radial keratotomy.

question: In what layer of the cornea is the pigmentation indicated by the arrow located and is it visually significant?
explanation: The brown pigmentation located centrally in this cornea and indicated by the white arrow represents a type of iron line seen in about 80% of patients with prior radial keratotomy. "Iron lines" form from epithelial iron deposition in areas with pooling of tears related to corneal surface irregularities. This particular iron line is sometimes referred to as a "tear star" because it can take on a star or "asterisk-like" appearance (not as evident in this photo). Iron lines are generally NOT visually significant. Additional well known corneal iron lines include: • "Hudson-Stahli line" which is located at the junction of the upper two thirds and lower one third of the cornea (i.e. at the tear meniscus) • "Ferry's line" at the leading edge of a filtering bleb • "Fleisher ring or line" surrounding the base of a cone in keratoconus • "Stocker's line" at the leading edge of a pterygium. Extra: • Mnemonic: Filter ferry, stocker ptery, fleisher keri, HS geri (as in geriatrics)

question: What layer of the cornea does the copper deposit in Wilson's disease as seen in the photo?
explanation: Wilson disease is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. The two classic ocular findings are the Kayser-Fleischer ring and the "sunflower" cataract. The Kayser-Fleischer ring is a brownish discoloration in the peripheral Descemet's membrane. Systemic treatment with D-penicillamine (which binds copper ions) can actually lead to a disappearance of the ring. The sunflower cataract is secondary to deposition of copper in the anterior capsule of the lens in a petaloid configuration. Extra:

question: Which of the following statements concerning Wilson disease is true:

options.D: posterior subcapsular cataracts are specific for Wilson Disease

explanation: Wilson disease is inherited autosomal recessively. The two classic ocular findings are the Kayser- Fleischer ring and the sunflower cataract. The Kayser-Fleischer ring is a brownish discoloration in the peripheral Descemet's membrane. There is decreased serum ceruloplasmin. Systemic treatment with penicillamine can actually lead to a disappearance of the ring. The sunflower cataract is secondary to deposition of copper in the anterior capsule of the lens in a petaloid configuration.

question: Which of the following medications is absorbed into the blood stream, goes to the aqueous and is then absorbed into the posterior cornea and anterior lens capsule resulting in pigment deposition?
explanation: Chlorpromazine (Thorazine) and thioridazine (Mellaril) are phenothiazines. These medications are absorbed in the blood stream and then make their way to the aqueous. From the aqueous they absorb into the posterior cornea and anterior lens capsule and result in pigment deposition. The incidence of this lens opacity depends on both drug dose and treatment duration. This lens opacity does not disappear even with discontinuing the medication, though it generally is visually insignificant. In the retina, chlorpromazine rarely causes damage. At doses normally used (<800 mg/day) thioridazine rarely causes retinopathy. But thioridazine can result in severe retinopathy with high doses. Initially there is RPE stippling in the posterior pole. It then progresses to RPE loss in a nummular (coin-shaped) pattern. Immediate cessation of the drug is indicated when retinopathy is detected. Chlorpromazine deposits on the anterior lens capsule.

question: Which of the following is the LEAST LIKELY to cause toxic ulcerative keratopathy?
explanation: Toxic ulcerative keratopathy is the condition caused by topically applied medications. It is due to impaired epithelial wound healing and manifests as a diffuse punctate keratitis which can lead to a persistent epithelial defect. The most common medications associated with this condition include: medications containing BAK, topical anesthetics, topical NSAIDs, trifluoridine, beta-blockers, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Thus, glaucoma patients presenting with persistent corneal epithelial problems should have their medications evaluated as a potential cause. Benzalkonium chloride (BAK) is a common preservative in topical medications that actually increases the potency of drugs by causing a disruption in corneal epithelial cells. Latanoprost is generally a well-tolerated topical medication. Trifluridine 1% (i.e. Viroptic®) is highly toxic to the epithelium and its extended use can result in neurotrophic ulcers. It should generally be stopped after 14 days. Brimonidine 0.2% (i.e. Alphagan®) can cause a follicular conjunctivitis in a large proportion (~15%) of patients. Lower concentrations (e.g. 0.1%) and the use of a non- BAK preservative (e.g. Purite®) help to lower the incidence of this side effec Ocular Immunology

question: Which of the following contribute to the cornea's relative immune isolation?

options.A: presence of blood vessels and lymphatics
options.B: downregulation of transforming growth factor betas

explanation: The cornea is considered to be an "immunologically privileged" site meaning that the responsiveness to foreign antigens is relatively suppressed. The BCSC states that this immune privilege can be attributed to the following factors: • Absence of blood vessels and lymphatics. This impairs the delivery of immune effectors cells and the flow of antigens to the draining lymph nodes. • Expression of immunosuppressive factors (e.g. TGF-beta, neuropeptides such as alpha-melanocyte stimulating hormone). • Expression of Fas ligand (CD95) by corneal cells. This increased expression is believed to be instrumental in causing Fas-mediated apoptosis of activated lymphocytes. • In general, there is a downregulation of MHC molecules within the cornea.

question: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome?
explanation: Type I immune reactions Are anaphylactic Or atopic reactions. In these reactions, preformed Ige antibodies bound on mast cell receptors react with the antigen causing degranulation of the mast cell with histamine release. An example of a Type I reaction is allergic conjunctivitis. Type II immune reactions are caused by cytotoxic antibodies. This reaction is where antibodies bind to foreign antigen and activate the complement pathway. An example of a type II reaction is ocular cicatricial pemphigoid. Type III immune reactions are also known as " immune-complex reactions." These reactions result from immune complex deposition in tissues which activate the complement and other effector systems. An example of a Type III reaction is "serum sickness", systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Previously, a copy of the BCSC (prior to 2016) fundamentals had listed Stevens Johnson syndrome as a type III reaction. Type IV immune reaction s are delayed hypersensitivity reactions. These involve recruitment of pre-sensitized immune cells. An example of a type IV reaction is allergic contact dermatitis. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome is now classified ed as a type IV immune reaction. Type V immune reactions are a newer class of hypersensitivity reactions called " stimulatory hypersensitivity." This type of reaction occurs when antibodies are produced with the property of stimulating specific cell targets. The most common example would be Graves’ disease which is characterized by antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor.

question: Which of the following are true about ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (OCP)?

options.A: autoantibodies are directed against bullous pemphigoid antigen II (BP180) in the basement membrane zone (BMZ)
options.B: it generally has a unilateral presentation
options.C: it is suggested by an inferior forniceal depth of less than 12 mm
options.D: methotrexate is frequently used over cyclophosphamide in severe cases of this disease

explanation: Ocular cicatrial pemphigoid is secondary to autoantibodies directed against bullous pemphigoid antigen II (BP180) in the basement membrane zone (BMZ). It is generally a bilateral disease. It is suggested by an inferior forniceal depth of less than 8 mm. Cyclophosphamide is frequently used in severe disease.

question: You are told that the patient in the photo had a biopsy of the conjunctiva and there were autoantibodies to the basement membrane zone. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen in the condition in the photo (see image)?
explanation: This is a picture of ocular cicatricial pemphigoid.

question: A 26-year-old gentleman is referred to you by his optometrist who noted new corneal infiltrates in the right eye.  Of note, the patient was being treated empirically with neomycin ointment after suffering a small corneal abrasion.  On exam, you note several small peripheral, ring-shaped corneal infiltrates in the inferior cornea of the right eye.   There is no epithelial defect overlying these infiltrates.  What type of hypersensitivity reaction do these infiltrates represent?
explanation: Neomycin is known to cause peripheral corneal infiltrates as a possible side effect. These infiltrates are a type of Wessely immune ring which represents the coalescence of local antibodies to antigens with subsequent complement activation. These immune rings are type 3 hypersensitivity reactions. Other conditions that may cause a Wessely ring include corneal foreign body and contact lens reactions. The classic ocular diseases that represent different hypersensitivity reactions include: • type 1 ("anaphylaxis"): allergic/atopic conjunctivitis • type 2 ("cytotoxic antibodies"): ocular cicatricial pemphigoid • type 3 ("immune-complex reactions"): scleritis • type 4 ("cell-mediated reactions"): contact dermatitis, corneal graft rejection, Stevens-Johnson syndrome. • type 5 ("stimulatory hypersensitivity"): thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis Note: older texts, including older versions of the BCSC have listed Stevens-Johnson Syndrome as type III, but recent papers in the literature have listed SJS as type IV. Given the controversy and recent changes, one would hope SJS classification would not be a good exam question.

question: Which of the following statements regarding vernal keratoconjunctivitis is TRUE?

options.A: the palpebral form has giant follicles
options.B: the palpebral form has Horner-Trantas dots
options.D: mast cell stabilizers are used for immediate relief

explanation: A good way of remembering vernal is to know that "vernal" means "Spring". This is a good way of remembering when vernal conjunctivitis occurs and that it is related to an allergic phenomena. This allergic entity typically occurs in children within the first 2 decades of life during the spring or fall. Classic ocular signs include: (1) giant papillary conjunctivitis; (2) "Horner- Trantas dots" which are jellylike limbal nodules representing degenerated eosinophils; and a (3) "shield ulcer" which is a corneal epithelial defect involving the upper half of the cornea. The palpebral form of vernal has giant papillae. The limbal form of vernal has Horner- Trantas dots. Mast cell stabilizers take at least 2 weeks to reach effect. Extra: Differential diagnosis The main differential diagnosis to be considered is atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC). AKC typically has an older age of onset in the 2nd to 5th decade, as opposed to onset prior to age 10 with VKC. Conjunctival involvement is classically on the upper tarsus in VKC and on the lower tarsus in AKC. Additionally, AKC is typically more chronic in nature and more commonly results in scarring of the cornea and conjunctival cicatrization, whereas VKC is typically more self-limiting

question: Which of the following is a common finding seen in atopic keratoconjunctivitis?

options.D: posterior subcapsular or anterior subcapsular cataracts

explanation: Approximately 1/3 of individuals with atopic dermatitis will develop atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC). Some of the characteristic findings in AKC include: • Small or medium-sized papillae (not giant like in vernal or contact-lens associated conjunctivitis) • Extensive corneal vascularization with opacification can occur • Year-round disease (in contrast to seasonal exacerbation that occurs in vernal) • Posterior subcapsular or multifaceted or shield-shaped anterior subcapsular cataracts The etiology of these cataracts is unknown but appears multi-factorial: AKC patients rub their eyes more often; use corticosteroids frequently; and they may have an immunologic response to skin epithelial cells which may cross-react to lens epithelial cells. Individuals with AKC also have depressed systemic cell-mediated immunity. Because of this, these patients are more susceptible to herpes simplex keratitis and colonization of the eyelids with Staphlococcus aureus. Giant papillae, Horner-Trantas dots, and shield ulcers are much more characteristic of vernal keratoconjunctivitis than of AKC.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of olopatadine?

options.B: It is a competitive antagonist against histamine receptors
options.C: It promotes the degranulation of mast cells

explanation: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is a very common allergic disease typically elicited by airborne allergens such as pollen, grass, weeds and animal dander. It is a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE in response to these environmental antigens. When specific allergens bind to sensitized mast cells in the conjunctiva, degranulation of mast cells, and release of preformed (histamine, eosinophil chemotactic factor, tryptase) and newly synthesized mediators (prostaglandins, leukotrines) occur. Olopatadine is a selective H1-receptor antagonist and inhibitor of mast cell degranulation. This agent has a rapid-onset due to antihistamine activity and prolonged duration of action due to mast cell stabilization. Its dual activity is an advantage and the drug may be used both as a therapeutic and prophylactic agent. Cyslosporine is a fungal metabolite that reduces ocular inflammation by inhibiting Th2 lymphocyte proliferation, interleukin-2 production, and histamine release from mast cells. Topical cyclosporine has been used successfully in the treatment of a number of ocular surface diseases. The improvement in tear film stability provided by topical cyclosporine and its anti-inflammatory effects on meibomian glands have been shown to be beneficial in patients with meibomian gland dysfunction. In addition, recent studies have shown that topical cyclosporine can be an effective anti-inflammatory treatment for vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis.

question: A 53-year-old patient with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with a painful eye. You note the corneal changes as seen in the photo above. Fluorescein staining reveals an epithelial defect on the cornea and the sclera. Which of the following is an accepted treatment for this patient's most likely condition?
explanation: This photo is most suggestive of peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK). PUK is a manifestation of autoimmune disease, the most common of which is rheumatoid arthritis. PUK generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients experience a lot of pain because of this epithelial loss. It can be hard to distinguish PUK from Moorens because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves the cornea. Moving the conjunctiva further from the limbus (i.e. conjunctival recession) also moves the feeder blood vessels further from the peripheral cornea. Since these blood vessels are the source of immunologic mediators, conjunctival recession will help relieve the corneal inflammation. Lastly, it is extremely important to address the underlying autoimmune disease with timely referral to the appropriate specialist (e.g. rheumatologist).

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK)?
explanation: PUK is seen in all of the answer choices. It is also seen in ulcerative colitis, relapsing polychondritis, rosacea, and other inflammatory diseases. The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. It generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients experience a lot of pain because of the epithelial loss. It can be difficult to distinguish PUK from Moorens ulcer because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves the cornea. Extra:

question: Which of the following statements about Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) is true:
explanation: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis is generally a very painful disease which helps distinguish it from Terrien's Marginal Degeneration. PUK is a manifestation of autoimmune disease. The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. It generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients have a lot of pain because of the epithelial loss. It can be hard to distinguish PUK from Moorens because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves cornea. Moving the conjunctiva further from the limbus also moves the feeding blood vessels further from the peripheral cornea. Blood vessels are the source of immunologic mediators. The most important treatment is to address the underlying system autoimmune disease. Terrien Marginal Degeneration is generally unilateral or asymmetrically bilateral. The cornea starts to thin superiorly and the thinning spreads circumferentially. The epithelium remains intact and a fine pannus traverses the area of corneal thinning. At the end of the pannus is a line of lipid deposition. Perforation of the thinned cornea is rare. Crescent shaped lamellar transplantation can be used if perforation does occur. It generally starts in the 2nd or 3rd decade of life.

question: A rheumatoid arthritis patient presents with a sterile painful peripheral ulcer with stromal thinning. Aggressive lubrication has been instituted and the stromal melt has continued from 10% thickness to 50% thickness over 2 weeks. What is the next best treatment modality indicated to prevent corneal perforation?

options.A: continued aggressive lubrication and punctal plug

explanation: This patient has Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis. Aggressive lubrication has not helped the patient thus far. Recessing the conjunctiva distances conjunctival blood vessels from carrying cell mediators to the peripheral cornea. Methotrexate or other cell mediator would be a good choice but they will not help the immediate situation. Methotrexate takes about 6-8 weeks to take effect. Tectonic grafting would not be indicated with only 50% thinning of the cornea.

question: Which of the following sign or symptom is not shared in Mooren Ulcer and Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK):
explanation: Scleral involvement is seen in PUK and not in Mooren Ulcer. PUK is a manifestation of autoimmune disease. The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. It generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients have a lot of pain because of the epithelial loss. It can be hard to distinguish PUK from Moorens because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves cornea. Moving the conjunctiva further from the limbus also moves the feeding blood vessels further from the peripheral cornea. Blood vessels are the source of immunologic mediators. The most important treatment is to address the underlying system autoimmune disease.

question: A medical student presents to your clinic with complaints of eye irritation. He just came back from an elective in India 2 weeks ago. He did recall a rather nasty bout of diarrhea while there after enjoying the authentic local cuisine. He also notes he is having difficulty urinating and ankle pain. What is the most likely eye finding on exam:
explanation: This patient developed Reactive Arthritis (aka Reiter Syndrome). Reactive arthritis may occur after gram-negative bacterial dysentery (most frequently associated with Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia) or after nongonococcal urethritis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. More than 75% of patients with reactive arthritis are HLA-B27 positive. Papillary conjunctivitis is the most common ocular manifestation. Extra: Could have iritis, but most common manifestation is papillary conjunctivitis

question: Which of the following lab tests are CLASSICALLY abnormal in Wegener's granulomatosis (aka granulomatosis with polyangiitis)?
explanation: One way of remembering this is to remember that cyclophosphamide is used to treatment Wegener's granulomatosis. Cyclophosphamide starts with a C just like c- ANCA. p-ANCA is classically abnormal in polyarteritis nodosa and inflammatory bowel disorder. c-ANCA, or cytoplasmic (classical) antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, show a diffusely granular, cytoplasmic staining pattern. The target antigen is most commonly proteinase 3 (PR3). p-ANCA, or peri-nuclear (protoplasmic-staining) antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, show a perinuclear staining pattern. The target antigen is most commonly myeloperoxidase (MPO). As many of you have commented, Friedrich Wegener was apparently affiliated with the Nazi party during World War II. Thus, his disease moniker has been replaced recently with "granulomatosis with polyangiitis."

question: A 30-year-old woman presents to you complaining of recurrent episodes of foreign body sensation, photophobia, burning, and tearing in both eyes for the past 5 years.  Each episode lasts for approximately 1 month.  Her slit-lamp exam is significant for the above corneal findings which are found in both eyes.  She has tried frequent artificial tears without relief.  She states that she cannot tolerate any form of corticosteroid including in eyedrops.  Which of the following is the best treatment choice for this patient's condition?
explanation: This patient presents with photophobia and foreign body sensation in the presence of a cluster of corneal epithelial lesions. These lesions would likely stain "negatively" with fluorescein. In addition, both eyes are affected and the lesions are concentrated centrally on both corneas. This is the classic presentation for Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis which first was described by Phillips Thygeson in 1950. The etiology of Thygeson's is currently unknown. The classic corneal findings consist of ~15-20 discrete, round/oval, punctate intraepithelial deposits that are concentrated in the central cornea. The conjunctival is mildly injected or entirely quiet. The bouts of foreign body sensation typically last ~1-2 months with a similar time period of remission. The best initial treatment for this disorder are artificial tears especially in mild-to- moderate cases. The corneal lesions are very sensitive to steroid treatment but have a high rate of recurrence once the drops are stopped. Conservative treatment is the best first-line approach. If artificial tears and corticosteroids are not effective and/or contraindicated, then one can consider alternative treatments such as: • cyclosporin eyedrops (e.g. 0.5% or 2%) • bandage contact lenses • tacrolimus (aka FK506) Fluoromethalone 0.1% (choice "A") would be effective, but is not an option for this patient since she absolutely cannot use corticosteroids. Lastly, epithelial debridement ("B") and ketorolac ("C") have not been shown to be effective for Thygeon's SPK.

question: A 30-year-old female patient presents to your clinic with a complaint of three weeks of light sensitivity in the left eye.  She states that the light sensitivity is fairly incapacitating and is associated with tearing and burning.  She states that she had a similar episode three years ago in the right eye and five years ago in the left eye, both of which self-resolved in several weeks.  The patient denies any sick contacts and denies current illness.
explanation: The patient’s vision is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left. On exam, you note minimal injection in both eyes and numerous, central, corneal intra-epithelial opacities that positively stain with fluorescein in the left eye. In the right eye, two such opacities are present. What is the natural history of the most likely diagnosis? A.Recurrences and remittances with ultimate self-resolution B.Progressive stromal melt leading to perforation C.Visually significant corneal scarring D.Neurotrophic ulceration A:A The clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of Thygeson’s superficial punctate keratitis (TSPK). TSPK presents as an epithelial keratitis with punctate erosions and underlying intra-epithelial opacities. The presentation is typically unilateral or asymmetrically bilateral. Stromal involvement does not occur. TSPK is marked by recurrences and remittances over its course, which may last years if not decades. Fortunately, the condition self-resolves in the vast majority of cases. At present, TSPK is considered idiopathic, though postviral and/or autoimmune etiologies are plausible. TSPK may be mistaken for epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) due to both presenting with punctate epitheliopathy and epithelial opacities. However, EKC typically presents with a great deal of conjunctival injection, and its subepithelial opacities do not concentrate in the central cornea. Patients with EKC also typically manifest some degree of systemic symptoms and/or signs. The treatment of TSPK centers on control of inflammation with topical corticosteroids as the mainstay of therapy. Frequently, corticosteroids cannot be fully discontinued due to a recurrence of the inflammation and may be maintained an infrequent instillation schedule. Topical immunomodulatory therapy, such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus, has also been investigated as alternative anti- inflammatory agents. Topical lubricants and therapeutic soft contact lenses assist with symptom relief. In regards to the other answer choices, progressive stromal melt leading to perforation is seen in peripheral ulcerative keratitis and Mooren's ulcer. Visual significant corneal scarring may occur in a host of corneal conditions. One condition that typically presents with such scarring is keratoconus, as the scarring occurs at the apex of the cone, often located paracentrally and adjacent to the visual axis. Neurotrophic ulceration classically occurs as a sequela of herpetic keratitis though may be seen in any condition or surgery that compromises the trigeminal nerve anywhere along its course from the brainstem to the cornea.

question: A patient presents with a 2 month history of eye irritation. On exam, there are thick pseudomembranes on both palpebral conjunctival surfaces with a woody appearance. What underlying biochemical defect is present?
explanation: Ligneous conjunctivitis is a very rare, autosomal recessive disorder that is caused by severe type 1 plasminogen deficiency. The genetic defect is in the plasminogen gene (PLG) on 6q26. It is characterized by the formation of "woody", yellowish pseudomembranes on the conjunctiva (typically, palpebral). These patients typically have ocular irritation and foreign body sensation. The deficiency in type 1 plasminogen leads to hypofibrinolysis and >12% of these individuals have severe hypoplasminogenemia. The membranes can be excised, but it is recommended to use adjuvant mitomycin-C (MMC) or an amniotic membrane graft at the time of excision. These membranes frequently recur after excision and may also spontaneously resolve after months-to- years. Extra:

question: A 23-year-old woman presents with stromal keratitis, vertigo, and hearing loss. You place the patient on topical corticosteroids. What other medication should you give the patient?
explanation: This patient is presenting with symptoms of Cogan syndrome. Cogan syndrome is an autoimmune disease that presents with hearing loss, vertigo, and stromal keratitis. It generally occurs in young adults who have had an upper respiratory tract infection in the previous one to two weeks. Topical steroids treat the keratitis and oral steroids treat the auditory system. It is very important for an Ophthalmologist to recognize the disease and its potential impact on the auditory system (i.e. deafness if not treated adequately). Because you never want to treat infectious stromal keratitis with oral nor topical steroids, it is important to rule out syphilis as a cause of the eye findings.

question: A 23-year-old woman presents with stromal keratitis, vertigo, and hearing loss. Which of the following laboratory values should you obtain?

options.B: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) to creatinine ratio
options.C: Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) or Rapid plasma reagin (RPR)

explanation: This patient is presenting with symptoms of Cogan syndrome. Cogan syndrome is an autoimmune disease that presents with hearing loss, vertigo, and stromal keratitis. It generally occurs in young adults who have had an upper respiratory tract infection in the previous one to two weeks. Topical steroids treat the keratitis and oral steroids treat the auditory system. It is very important for an Ophthalmologist to recognize the disease and its potential for deafness if left untreated. Because you never want to treat infectious stromal keratitis with oral or topical steroids, it is important to rule out syphilis as a cause of the eye findings. As a refresher, stromal keratitis associated with congenital syphilis is generally bilateral and unilateral with acquired syphilis.

question: Q- Mikulicz syndrome is the combination of which of the following:

options.A: lacrimal gland enlargement, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and liver enlargement
options.B: lacrimal gland enlargment, salivary gland enlargement, and keratoconjunctivitis sicca
options.C: salivary gland enlargement, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and posterior blepharitis
options.D: lacrimal gland enlargment, salivary gland enlargement, and posterior blepharitis

explanation: Mikulicz syndrome is a combination of lacrimal gland enlargement, salivary gland enlargement, and keratoconjunctivitis sicca.

question: Lofgren syndrome is the combination of which of the following:

options.A: submental adenopathy, erythema nodosum, and iridocyclitis
options.B: lacrimal gland enlargement, hilar adenopathy, and erythema nodosum
options.C: hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum, and arthritis
options.D: lacrimal gland enlargment, submental adenopathy, and iridocycliti

explanation: This is a manifestation of systemic sarcoidosis. The other commonly tested systemic sarcoid condition is Heerfordt syndrome which is a combination of uveitis, parotitis, fever, and facial nerve palsy.

question: Heerfordt syndrome is the combination of all of the following:

options.A: lacrimal gland enlargement, uveitis, and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy
options.B: fever, uveitis, and facial nerve palsy
options.D: hilar adenopathy, uveitis, and erythema nodosum

explanation: "Heerfordt syndrome" is a specific type of systemic sarcoidosis. It is characterized by a granulomatous uveitis (as seen by mutton-fat keratic precipitates), constitutional symptoms (including respiratory symptoms), parotid swelling, and facial nerve paralysis. "Lofgren syndrome" is another form of systemic sarcoidosis and is defined by the combination of bilateral hilar adenopathy, arthropathy, fever, and erythema nodosum. "Mikulicz syndrome" is a combination of lacrimal gland enlargement, salivary gland enlargement, and keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Immune-related Disorders of the External Eye

question: A 77-year-old Caucasian woman is referred for a "pigmented mass" of the right eye. The woman states that this lesion has been present for the past 2 months. The woman does not complain of photophobia or eye pain. There are no abnormalities seen on ultrasound biomicroscopy, B-scan, or CT scan. Which of the following is associated with the most likely underlying systemic disorder?

options.A: positive titer for autoantibodies against IgG
options.D: positive titer for anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)

explanation: The slit-lamp photo demonstrates uveal tissue protruding through an area of severe scleral thinning. There appears to be only a very thin layer of conjunctiva overlying the uveal tissue. This finding is most consistent with a diagnosis of scleromalacia perforans. This entity is sometimes also called "necrotizing scleritis without inflammation" since patients with this condition rarely have eye pain or other signs typical of the other forms of anterior scleritis. Most patients with scleromalacia perforans have rheumatoid arthritis, which is a systemic autoimmune disease associated with a positive rheumatoid factor (RF). RF is actually an autoantibody directed against IgG. One important thing to note is that if you diagnose a patient with scleromalacia perforans, the patient requires a referral for a systemic workup since the underlying autoimmune disease is almost always present and can be associated with significant morbidity. Anti-recoverin antibodies are found in patients with "carcinoma-associated retinopathy"; ANA is positive in many patients, but is most commonly found in lupus patients; ANCA can also be found in a variety of diseases, the most prominent of which are Wegener's granulomatosis and polyarteritis nodosa.

question: Which of the following signs or symptoms is MOST LIKELY to be seen in a patient with scleromalacia perforans?
explanation: Scleromalacia perforans is generally painless with minimal inflammation and rarely spontaneously perforates. However, it is associated with globe rupture after minimal trauma.

question: Which of the following most accurately describes scleromalacia perforans?
explanation: Necrotizing scleritis without inflammation" which is also known as "scleromalacia perforans." This entity is said to be "without inflammation" because, unlike the other forms of anterior scleritis, this scleritis presents with minimal inflammation and minimal pain. When an associated systemic condition can be identified, patients with scleromalacia perforans classically have rheumatoid arthritis. It is important to co-manage these patients with a rheumatologist since the often-underlying autoimmune condition is associated with significant mortality if not properly treated. The answer image shows an eye with scleromalacia perforans with marked thinning of the sclera temporally with bulging of the underlying uveal tissue. Large blood vessels oftentimes cross the area of scleral loss.

question: A 28-year-old woman, with a history of sinusitis, presents with the findings shown above.  What is the diagnosis?
explanation: This patient has necrotizing scleritis with inflammation (answer C). The sclera is diffusely inflamed and there is a broad area of avascular, necrotic sclera. Necrotizing scleritis in a young patient with a history sinusitis should prompt a workup for granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Immunomodulatory therapy such as cyclophosphamide is often warranted in such severe cases. These patients have a high mortality rate from systemic vasculitis if not adequately treated. WRONG ANSWERS: • As its name suggests, non-necrotizing diffuse anterior scleritis presents with diffuse inflammation but does not display necrosis (answer A). • Nodular anterior scleritis presents with a focal nodule without necrosis (answer B). • Necrotizing scleritis without inflammation, or scleromalacia perforans, is often seen in patients with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis. There is typically much less inflammation or pain compared to the other forms of scleritis. Patients often have diffuse scleral thinning with visible underlying uveal tissue. In advanced cases, these eyes may rupture with minimal trauma.

question: You have just removed a pterygium and debate what you should do next.  Which of the following surgical techniques is associated with the highest rate of pterygium recurrence?
explanation: Simply leaving the area involved by the pterygium open (i.e. "bare sclera", choice C) is unacceptable in most circumstances and should be avoided at all costs. It is reported to have a 24-89% rate of pterygium recurrence. Simple closure may be done if no available amniotic membrane (eg, financial reasons) or conjunctival tissue (eg, severe glaucoma where conjunctival tissue is needed for upcoming filtering procedure, or severe ocular surface disease where the conjunctiva is unhealthy, etc) is unavailable. This may not be possible in most cases of pterygium removal as the resulting conjunctival defect may be too large to close with simple closure. Still, this technique is preferred over the bare sclera approach. Closing the conjunctiva with amniotic membrane has the advantage of preserving conjunctiva for future ocular surgeries (eg, pterygium, glaucoma, etc). The exact mechanism by which the amniotic membrane prevents recurrence has not been fully elucidated, but it is thought that the graft contains anti-inflammatory mediators that inhibit fibrosis and recurrence. The recurrence rates vary widely among the published studies in the literature, ranging from 3-10% for primary pterygia and as high as 37.5% for recurrent pterygia. Conjunctival autograft is the preferred method of most surgeons whenever possible as recurrence rates are as low as 2%, though the percentages have ranged widely in the literature. Recurrence rates for sliding conjunctival autograft range from 3.2% to 10.7% and for free conjunctival autograft rates vary from 0% to 39% among different reports. Autograft is especially preferred for recurrent pterygia, and the literature suggests that further augmenting conjunctival autograft with limbal stem cell transplantation for severe, recurrent cases, may confer additional benefits to decrease the risk of recurrence. The take home message from this is that the literature varies about the EXACT recurrence rates among using AMT vs. the type of conjunctival autograft. However, bare sclera definitively has the HIGHEST recurrence rate and should be avoided at all costs. Extra: Differences: Pinguecula vs Pterygium Disease Entity Pterygium, from the Greek pterygos meaning “wing”, is a common ocular surface lesion originating in the limbal conjunctiva within the palpebral fissure with progressive involvement of the cornea. The lesion occurs more frequently at the nasal limbus than the temporal with a characteristic wing-like appearance. Signs The diagnosis of pterygium is based on the clinical appearance of the lesion. Typical findings include • Fibrovascular conjunctival growth within the palpebral fissure extending onto the corneal surface • triangular or trapezoidal shape with the apex, or head, extending onto the cornea • vascular straightening in the direction of the advancing head of the pterygium on the corneal surface. • It may affect the nasal and temporal limbus of both eyes or only a single location. • Raised lesion, white to pink in color depending on vascularity • Ranges from a fine transparent area with very mild elevation, few vessels, and minimal corneal involvement in the early stages to a thick opaque vascular growth extending to the visual axis in later stages • Pinguecula are often present in the ipsilateral or contralateral eye • A pigmented epithelial iron line (Stocker’s line) adjacent to a pterygium is evidence of chronicity. Surgery Excision with conjunctival autograft is considered the current gold standard because of its low rate of recurrence. This approach carries an approximate rate of recurrence of 5-10% with minimal risk of complications.. Excision with amniotic membrane graft can be considered as an alternative to conjunctival autograft, though recurrence rates are still higher than rates with conjunctival autograft. Simple excision with bare sclera or conjunctival closure will result in a recurrence rate as high as 80% and is now considered unacceptable. Excision together with adjunctive therapies such as mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil can reduce the risk of recurrence to approximately 10%, However, the use of mitomycin C and 5-fluorouracil can increase the risk of corneal or scleral melt postoperatively

question: A 66-year-old Caucasian man presents to you with complaints of left eye pain especially when looking toward his right. He states that his left eye has been red and painful for the past few weeks, and he also has some mildly decreased vision in this eye. He describes this eye like "a severe toothache that keeps me up at night." His slit-lamp exam of this eye is seen above and is notable for non-blanching of the engorged vessels with phenylephrine. Which of the following treatments is presently most controversial for this condition?
explanation: This clinical vignette describes the classic signs and symptoms of scleritis (type not specified). In scleritis, the pain is the most dominant feature that causes most patients to seek medical advice. This pain is described as "boring" in nature, prevents one from sleeping well, and often radiates to other areas (e.g. temple). The inflammation in scleritis appears bluish-red in contrast to episcleritis which is a brighter-red. There is edema or necrosis of the sclera with an overlying episcleral edema. Occasionally, if the scleral edema cannot be visualized because of the overlying episcleral inflammation, then blanching with phenylephrine eyedrops can be performed. Treatment for most forms of scleritis typically begins with an oral NSAID (e.g. flurbiprofen, ibuprofen, naproxen, indomethacin). If there is a poor response (e.g. with 48 hours) to the first NSAID, then a different NSAID is used. In recalcitrant cases or those that are very severe or necrotizing, then systemic steroid therapy (e.g. prednisone 60-100 mg) is mandatory. For the most severe, vision-threatening bouts of scleritis, intravenous methylprednisolone can be used. Other non-steroid immunosuppressives (e.g. cyclophosphamide) are typically used if the aforementioned therapies fail or if the scleritis is part of a systemic inflammatory disorder (e.g. Wegener granulomatosis). Subconjunctival and/or depot (sub-Tenon's) corticosteroids are currently controverisal for treatment of scleritis since some believe they may exacerbate the inflammatory reaction in the sclera. This exacerbation is thought to lead to scleral perforation in some cases. However, some more recent data provides some evidence in support of subconjunctival corticosteroids in the treatment of non-necrotizing diffuse and nodular anterior scleritis. For example, a recent retrospective, multicenter study examined the effects of subconjunctival triamcinolone (STI) for patients already being treated for diffuse or nodular anterior scleritis with topical and/or systemic medications.1 This study enrolled 68 eyes of 53 patients and found that STI improved and completely resolved the signs and symptoms in 97% and 89.7% of patients respectively. Most importantly, no episodes of scleral thinning or necrosis were reported. Please note that this study did not enroll nor recommend the use of STI for patients with necrotizing scleritis. Extra:

question: Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for non-necrotizing diffuse anterior scleritis?
explanation: Scleritis generally does not respond to topical therapy. Oral NSAIDs are a good first choice for non-necrotizing scleritis. Subconjunctival injection of steroids would be contraindicated given the risk of scleral thinning.
