More severe nodular and necrotizing disease typically requires more intensive treatment with oral/intravenous corticosteroids or other powerful immunosuppressives (e.g., methotrexate, cyclosporine).

question: A 12-year-old girl presents with a painful red eye as shown above.  The vessels do not blanch with application of topical phenylephrine.  The remainder of the exam is within normal limits.  Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: The patient in the photo above has non-necrotizing, diffuse anterior scleritis. Unlike in episcleritis, the dilated vessels in scleritis are not blanched with phenylephrine. Oral NSAIDs (eg indomethacin, flurbiprofen, naproxen) are the first line treatment for non-necrotizing diffuse anterior scleritis in most cases (answer B). Typically, a second NSAID can be trialed prior to switching to corticosteroid treatment. Ocular Surface Disease

question: Which of the following can be seen in familial dysautonomia (Riley-Day Syndrome)?
explanation: Riley-Day syndrome patients can have an Ashkenazi family history, skin blotching, and neurotrophic keratopathy with decreased tearing when crying. This syndrome is also on the differential diagnosis of patients with enlarged corneal nerves. It is not associated with the other answer choices. Extra: Disease Entity an unusual clinical entity in children of Ashkenazi Jewish descent characterized by extensive sensory and autonomic abnormalities, including diminished tear production, excessive sweating and salivation, red blotching of the skin, reduced deep tendon reflexes, and marked arterial hypo/hypertension. [1] This entity became known as Riley Day syndrome, or more commonly referred to as familial dysautonomia (FD). Over the following decades, FD is now classified as one of the neurodevelopmental disorders termed hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies (HSAN) and is also termed HSAN-III. [ Neuro-ophthalmic Manifestations Notably, the most common ocular manifestation in FD patients is neurogenic alacrima (abnormal tear production). Furthermore, children with FD often have corneal hypesthesia, as part of the generalized neuropathy, that renders them insensitive to ocular pain caused by foreign bodies or other irritants. Lagophthalmos may also be present. Combined, these manifestations place FD patients at high risk of corneal epithelial defects that chronically progress to corneal abrasions and eventual corneal scarring

question: A delle (plural is dellen) generally occurs centripetally to a raised conjunctiva area. What layers of the cornea are absent with a delle?
explanation: Delle (plural is dellen) are saucerlike areas of corneal depression adjacent to raised areas of conjunctiva. There is thinning of the epithelium and stroma secondary to drying due to a poor blink. Rehydration of epithelium and stroma leads to minimal loss of thickness. Extra: • Clinical photograph of corneal dellen after nasal pterygium excision with conjunctival graft secured using tissue glue. The slit beam demonstrates thinning of the cornea. An epithelial defect was present. Dellen resolved with return to normal stromal thickness using a bandage contact lens and topical antibiotic and steroid drops. Disease “Dellen” dimple was first described by Ernst Fuchs as shallow, saucer-like excavations at the margin of the cornea. They are thought to occur due to localized tear film instability especially the mucin layer and dehydration. A delle: "Hello, it's me. I've been wondering 'bout the cornea, thinner than it used to be. These lids don't cover, everything They say that lube's supposed to heal ya But I ain't done much healing..."

question: Which of the following bacteria can classically penetrate an intact corneal epithelium?
explanation: The bacteria that classically penetrate an intact corneal epithelium are Neisseria gonorrhoeae or meningitidis, Haemophilus aegyptus, Shigella species, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and Listeria. This fact can be remembered by the mnemonic: "No Hard or Soft Contact Lenses" or "H and N Can Lyse whole Skin." H. aegyptus is not listed by the BCSC as one of the classic bacteria that penetrate an intact epithelium, so you are likely not going to have to remember this. Another mnemonic that you can use is: CHANLS (channels): Corynebacterium, Haemophilus Aegyptus, Neisseria, Listeria, Shigel la

question: Which bacteria species is associated with the foamy conjunctival lesion seen in the photo above?
explanation: This foamy lesion on the bulbar conjunctiva is called a "Bitot spot." It is caused by systemic vitamin A deficiency which leads to loss of mucus production by the conjunctival goblet cells. This lesion is composed of keratinized epithelium, debris, inflammatory cells, and the bacterium Corynebacterium xerosis. The bacteria release gas as a byproduct. Actinomyces israelii is the organism most commonly associated with canaliculitis. Streptococcus viridans is the organism most commonly associated with infectious crystalline keratopathy. This is a peculiar infection that occurs in post-penetrating keratoplasty corneas. It is characterized by "branching colonies of organisms" without an inflammatory response. Extra: Earliest symptom of hypovitaminosis a= nyctalopia Disease Xerophthalmia refers to the spectrum of ocular disease caused by severe Vitamin A deficiency (VAD). Vitamin A serves several essential functions in the eye, and deficiency can lead to a constellation of ocular signs and symptoms that affect the conjunctiva, cornea, and retina. Xerophthalmia continues to be a leading cause of preventable blindness in developing countries[1]. Unfortunately, xerophthalmia signifies a severity of VAD that causes significant morbidity and mortality from malnutrition and increased susceptibility to mucosal infections Bitot spots (Grade X1B): Bitot spots are collections of desquamated, keratinized epithelial cells mixed with the gas-forming bacteria Corynebacterium xerosis. They appear as triangular patches of foamy, whitish, opaque deposits, typically located on the bulbar conjunctiva near the limbus at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions. They are more common temporally.

question: Which of the following conditions is associated with the underlying disease causing the finding demonstrated in the photo above?
explanation: This is a Bitot spot secondary to vitamin A deficiency. The bacteria (Corynebacterium xerosis) release gas as a byproduct and produce the foamy conjunctival lesion. They can present with keratomalacia (corneal necrosis), nyctalopia (i.e. scotopic vision loss), and xerosis (dryness of the conjunctiva and cornea). Because they have dry eye, they have decreased tear break-up times. Extra: Conjunctival xerosis (Grade X1A): Conjunctival xerosis is characterized by a dull and dry appearance of the conjunctiva with slight wrinkling. It is caused by the loss of goblet cells and insufficient mucin secretion, and it can be subtle and difficult to detect clinically.

question: Which of the following is a known association with contact lenses:

options.A: hard contact lens overwear can lead to central epithelial edema
options.C: hard contact lenses can be associated with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK)
options.D: modern contact lens cleaning solutions leading to superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK)

explanation: There are many complications of contact lenses with which ophthalmologists must be familiar. Hard contact lenses can lead to central epithelial edema. This can be treated by discontinuing lens use. A micropannus of 1-2 mm is very common with soft contact lens use. The patient has to be carefully monitored if a micropannus develops. Often, a lens holiday is necessary or switching the lens to one with higher oxygen transmissibility. An older compound called thimerosal was used to clean contact lenses and was associated with SLK (superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis). This compound is no longer used. SLK is thought to be due to mechanical trauma of the upper eyelid on the superior limbal area. It is generally seen in adult women. It is often asymmetrically bilateral. Clinically, a papillary reaction occurs on the palpebral conjunctiva. There is hypertrophy of the superior conjunctiva, punctate epithelial erosions on the superior conjunctival and corneal epithelium, and sometimes a fine superior corneal pannus. It can be associated with thyroid abnormalities and therefore obtaining TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free T4 levels are recommended. Treatment involves aggressive lubrication, resection of the conjunctiva, large diameter soft contact lenses, cauterization of the conjunctiva, and Restasis (topical cyclosporine). Hard contact lens wear is not generally associated with the development of SLK

question: Which of the following is a term used to describe epithelial edema generally found after hard contact lens use?
explanation: Sattler's veil is central corneal epithelial edema due to contact lens use. It is generally secondary to PMMA hard contact lens use. Hard contacts result in a hypoxic state, lactate accumulation, and impaired carbon dioxide efflux. This process can be reversed by cessation of contact lens use. Another contact lens complication of the epithelium is microcystic epitheliopathy seen most often in extended wear soft contact lenses. It is seen as fine epithelial cysts. Discontinuing contact lenses use can cause them to disappear (but can take up to 6 weeks).

question: Which of the following statements about superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is FALSE?

options.A: Resection of the conjunctiva is contraindicated
options.B: It has been associated with thyroid disease
options.C: It results from upper eyelid mechanical trauma
options.D: It generally occurs bilaterally in adult women

explanation: SLK is thought to be due to mechanical trauma of the upper eyelid on the superior limbal area. It is generally seen in adult women and is often asymmetrically bilateral. Clinically, a papillary reaction occurs on the palpebral conjunctiva. There is hypertrophy of the superior conjunctiva, punctate epithelial erosions on the superior conjunctival and corneal epithelium, and sometimes a fine superior corneal pannus. It can be associated with thyroid abnormalities and TSH and free T4 levels are recommended. Treatment involves aggressive lubrication, resection of the conjunctiva, large diameter soft contact lenses, cauterization of the conjunctiva, and topical cyclosporine (i.e. Restasis).

question: A patient presents with progressively "cloudy" vision in his right eye associated with redness and photophobia.  As part of your diagnostic workup, you instill fluorescein and examine his cornea with a cobalt blue light.  You note late staining of the corneal epithelium with a "wavelike" irregularity.  What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
explanation: The corneal epithelial cells are continuously replaced through proliferation of a subpopulation of cells located in the basal layer of the limbus. This subpopulation of cells are called limbal stem cells. An individual must have approximately 25-33% of their limbal stem cell population to be intact to be able to maintain a normal ocular surface. There are many causes of limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) which include: • chemical burns • ocular surgery (e.g. multiple pterygium excisions) • long-term contact lens wear • Steven-Johnson syndrome, mucuous membrane pemphigoid • infections (e.g. herpes) • aniridia Patients with LSCD often complain of redness, photophobia, irritation, and decreased vision. Early slit-lamp findings of this condition include loss of the palisades of Vogt, peripheral pannus formation, and late staining of the epithelium (i.e. a "wavelike" irregularity). More advanced cases can lead to punctate epithelial keratopathy to frank, persistent epithelial defects. These epithelial defects can lead to stromal loss (i.e. ulcers), stromal scarring, and even corneal perforation. In limbal stem cell deficiency, the conjunctiva can grow onto the cornea to fill epithelial defects. This "conjunctivization" of the cornea is an indication for limbal stem cell deficiency and gives this unusual fluorescein staining pattern. Extra: Disease The corneal epithelium is a stratified squamous epithelium from which superficial terminal cells are naturally shed. Limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) is characterized by a loss or deficiency of the stem cells in the limbus that are vital for re-population of the corneal epithelium and to the barrier function of the limbus.[1][2] When these stem cells are lost, the corneal epithelium is unable to repair and renew itself. This results in epithelial breakdown and persistent epithelial defects, corneal conjunctivalization and neovascularization, corneal scarring, and chronic inflammation. All of these contribute to loss of corneal clarity, potential vision loss, chronic pain, photophobia, and keratoplasty failure Signs Patients present with progressive epitheliopathy with hazy, translucent epithelium extending centrally from the limbus, most commonly from the superior limbus. Epithelial staining, from punctate changes to more confluent staining, is broadest adjacent to the involved limbus and extends centripetally into the cornea to varying degrees in a whorl shape.[

question: What minimal percentage of corneal epithelial limbal stem cells must remain intact in order to properly replenish the corneal epithelium?
explanation: The histologic hallmark of LSCD is the presence of conjunctival goblet cells in the corneal epithelium. This histologic diagnosis is typically made with "impression cytology" whereby a piece of nitrocellulose filter paper is pressed onto the cornea and then examined under the microscope.

question: Which of the following findings is considered the hallmark of corneal limbal stem cell deficiency?

options.A: presence of fibroblasts along the palisades of Vogt
options.B: presence of conjunctival epithelium along the palisades of Vogt
options.C: presence of goblet cells on impression cytology of the cornea
options.D: presence of neutrophils or lymphocytes on impression cytology of the cornea

explanation: The corneal limbal stem cells are located in the basal layer of the limbus in a region called the "palisades of Vogt," which are a series of fibrovascular ridges perpendicular to the corneal margin. These ridges are located approximately 1-2 mm posterior to the limbus where the conjunctiva and Tenons capsule fuse. These limbal stem cells divide asymmetrically to produce one daughter cell and one stem cell. Thus, the stem cell population remains static in healthy corneas. The daughter cells differentiate and migrate to replenish the corneal surface. The corneal epithelium is completely regenerated in approximately 7 days. The hallmark of limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) is the presence of conjunctival goblet cells in the corneal epithelium (please commit this high yield fact to memory!). To demonstrate the presence of these cells, the clinician can either perform an excisional biopsy of the corneal surface or impression cytology and use a PAS or Alcian blue stain for goblet cells. Impression cytology is typically preferred since it is easier to perform and less invasive. Impression cytology basically involves pressing a piece of nitrocellulose filter paper against the corneal surface and staining whatever cells stick to the paper with the aforementioned dyes. The presence of conjunctival epithelial cells (or their markers; e.g. cytokeratin 19) on the corneal surface from impression cytology is another sign of LSCD. Clinical signs of LSCD are: • "effacement" or loss of the palisades of Vogt • late staining of the corneal epithelium with fluorescein • peripheral pannus or corneal neovascularization

question: A 50 year old patient presents to clinic with a severe alkali corneal burn in one of his eyes.  You are debating performing a limbal stem cell transplantation in the affected eye.  Assuming the patient is not showing any signs of epithelial improvement and there is no inflammation, how early after injury can a limbal stem cell transplantation be performed on the affected eye?
explanation: Limbal stem cell transplantation can be performed as soon as 2 weeks after chemical injury. Reducing inflammation prior to transplantation will increase the graft's odds of survival because inflammation leads to death of cells and a less favorable prognosis. This theory applies to corneal transplants as well.

question: Which of the following medications is associated with poor corneal epithelial wound healing?
explanation: Topical trifluridine (brand name: Viroptic) should generally be discontinued after a maximum of 14 days during the treatment of herpetic epithelial disease. The reason for this is that it is toxic to the epithelium and can contribute toward neurotrophic keratopathy. Other medications associated with poor corneal epithelial wound healing include topical ß-blockers (e.g. timolol) and topical NSAIDs (e.g. ketorolac). Please note that answer choices "A" and "D" are incorrect since these oral medications do not lead to poor corneal would healing. Topical cyclosporine (brand name: Restasis) is a common dry eye treatment and does not impair corneal epithelial wound healing.

question: It is thought that appropriate corneal CN V innervation releases trophic substances that help in the turnover of epithelial cells. Lack of this innervation is caused most by which of the following:
explanation: Topical ß blockers, topical CAIs, topical anesthetic abuse, topical NSAIDs, topical trifluridine (Viroptic), and corneal herpes zoster can all lead to neurotrophic ulcers. In addition, drops containing the preservative Benzalconium Chloride (BAK) cause neurotrophic keratopathy. Extra: NeuroTrophic ABC N: NSAIDS T: Trifluridine A: anesthetics B: Beta blockers C: CAI

question: Secondary sjogren syndrome is most commonly associated with which systemic condition:
explanation: Sjogrens syndrome is secondary to inflammation with secondary dysfunction of the lacrimal and salivary glands. Secondarily, rheumatoid arthritis is the most common cause. Extra: Disease Sjögren syndrome is a chronic inflammatory disorder characterized by exocrine gland dysfunction and a variable systemic course. Lymphocytic infiltration of the lacrimal and salivary glands results in the classic sicca complex characterized by dry eyes (keratitis sicca or keratoconjunctivitis sicca [KCS]) and dry mouth (xerostomia). Exocrine dysfunction at other sites may result in dryness symptoms involving the skin, nose, throat, trachea, or vagina. Systemic complications may develop, resulting in disease or dysfunction of the heart, lungs, liver, renal system, nervous system, muscles, joints, skin, vasculature, and blood. An increased incidence of lymphoma is well documented, and a subset of patients with certain clinical variables demonstrates increased mortality (purpura, mixed monoclonal cryoglobulinemia, and low C4 levels). Severe dry eyes can cause corneal scarring, ulceration, infection, and even perforation; thus, although the prognosis is good for most patients with Sjögren syndrome and ophthalmologic features, individuals with complications have a guarded prognosis.The differential diagnosis includes conditions such as adult blepharitis, dry eye syndrome, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis uveitis, as well keratopathies (superficial punctate, filamentary, neurotrophic, exposure).

question: Which one of the following statements about Sjogren's syndrome is true:

options.A: associated with macrophage infiltration of the lacrimal gland
options.B: can have ANA, SS-A, and SS-B autoantibodies
options.C: topical B-blockers can improve dry eye symptoms
options.D: diamox can improve dry eye symptoms

explanation: It is associated with lymphocytic infiltration of the lacrimal gland. Topical ß-blockers and diamox can worsen dry eye symptoms. ANA, SS-A, and SS-B are screening antibodies for Sjogren's.

question: Mooren's ulcer has been "classically" associated with which of the following?
explanation: It is thought that certain types of infections may trigger an immune response that then cross-reacts with corneal auto-antigens. This is a similar phenomenon that is thought to occur with Reiter's syndrome (occuring after gram negative dysentery). The preferred term for Reiter's syndrome is now "reactive arthritis". Mooren ulcer has been "classically" associated with helminthic infection (parasitic worms). Tapeworms, roundworms (e.g. hookworms), and flukes are the three main types of helminthic infections. There may be a loose association of Mooren's ulcer with TB, but it is not a classic one. The other classic association is between Mooren's ulcer and hepatitis C infection. Scleral involvement is seen in peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK), but not in Mooren Ulcer. PUK is a manifestation of autoimmune disease. The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. It generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients have a lot of pain because of the epithelial loss. It can be hard to distinguish PUK from Moorens because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves cornea.

question: Which of the following are characteristics of Mooren ulcer:

options.A: leading undermined edge of tissue with overlying intact epithelium

explanation: Mooren ulcer by definition has no underlying systemic autoimmune conditions. Scleral involvement is seen in PUK and not in Mooren Ulcer. PUK is a manifestation of autoimmune disease. The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. It generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients have a lot of pain because of the epithelial loss. It can be hard to distinguish PUK from Moorens because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves cornea. Moving the conjunctiva further from the limbus also moves the feeding blood vessels further from the peripheral cornea. Blood vessels are the source of immunologic mediators. The most important treatment is to address the underlying systemic autoimmune disease.

question: Which of the following systemic conditions has been associated with a "Mooren-like" Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis:
explanation: Interferon therapy to treat this Hep C associated Mooren-like PUK has shown some positive results. Therefore, ruling out Hep C is something to look for in patients presenting with a Mooren-like PUK. PUK is a manifestation of autoimmune disease. The most common cause is rheumatoid arthritis. It generally presents unilaterally as a peripheral corneal infiltration with epithelial loss. Patients have a lot of pain because of the epithelial loss. It can be hard to distinguish PUK from Moorens because of their similar clinical picture. However, PUK involves both the cornea and the sclera whereas Mooren's ulcer only involves cornea. HSV, VZV, TB, gonorrhea, syphilis, AIDs, and others have been associated with PUK. But the "Mooren-like" PUK is particularly associated with Hep C. The point of this question is to rule out potentially treatable systemic associations (particularly Hep C) if you diagnose PUK. Moving the conjunctiva further from the limbus also moves the feeding blood vessels further from the peripheral cornea. Blood vessels are the source of immunologic mediators. The most important treatment is to address the underlying system autoimmune disease.

question: Which of the following ocular and systemic disease associations is correct?

options.C: Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis; Systemic lupus erythematosus
options.D: Central cloudy dystrophy of Francois; Hyperlipidemia

explanation: Ocular disease and systemic disease associations are a high yield topic and should be committed to memory. The following are all accurate ocular disease / systemic disease associations: • Cogan’s syndrome (autoimmune interstitial keratitis and hearing loss) = polyarteritis nodosa • "Mooren ulcer"-type PUK = Hepatitis C • Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis = autoimmune thyroid disease • Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy = hyperlipidemia / hypercholesterolemia Patients that have Hepatitis C and present with what appears to be a Mooren ulcer should be assumed to have Hepatitis C-associated "Mooren ulcer"-type PUK. Thus, their Hepatitis should be treated first. In the past, ulcers in these patients have responded to interferon therapy. Recently approved nucleotide analogs (e.g. Sovaldi) can actually cure patients with HCV and would likely be the best choice. Extra: Disease Entity Mooren’s ulcer is characterized by painful peripheral corneal ulceration of unknown etiology. The disease generally begins with intense limbal inflammation and swelling in the episclera and conjunctiva [1]. Corneal changes begin within 2-3 mm from the limbus, first appearing as grey swellings that rapidly furrow, affecting the superficial one-third of the cornea and then proceeding circumferentially and centrally over 4-12 months. Gottsch and colleagues have suggested that this disorder can result from a host response to calgranulin C,

question: Which of the following is seen with neurotrophic corneal ulcers?
explanation: Neurotrophic ulcers are described as being round and having heaped-up elevated edges generally in the inferonasal location because of the Bell's phenomenon. They are commonly associated with HSV or VZV. They are not associated with Fuchs dystrophy. Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) generally occurs bilaterally in adult women. It is thought to be due to upper eyelid mechanical trauma. It can be associated with thyroid eye disease and serologic tests (e.g. TSH, free T4) are indicated if SLK is suspected. The most common causes of neurotrophic keratopathy include: • aneurysms • stroke • CN V damage (trauma, large limbal incision, corneal nerve damage from PKP, LASIK, etc) • Diabetes • Familial dysautonomia (Riley-Day syndrome) • HSV • VZV • leprosy (Hansen disease) • multiple sclerosis • topical medication toxicity (anesthetics, glaucoma drops, NSAIDs, drops with BAK) • tumors (acoustic neuroma, angioma, neurofibroma) Treatments include: cessation of offending drops, artificial tears, serum drops (20%), punctal plugs, patching, low water content soft contact lenses, scleral hard contact lenses, amniotic membrane, and tarsorrhaphy. Extra: Disease Neurotrophic Keratitis (NK) is a corneal degenerative disease characterized by a reduction or absence of corneal sensitivity. In NK, corneal innervation by the trigeminal nerve is impaired. Partial or complete loss of corneal sensation may result in epithelial keratopathy, epithelial defect, stromal ulceration, and eventually corneal perforation. physical Examination Clinical presentation of NK ranges from subtle corneal surface irregularities to corneal melting and perforation. NK is usually graded in three different stages according to the “Mackie classification”.[16] • Stage I is characterized by epithelial irregularity most commonly in the form of punctate keratopathy without epithelial defect. • • Stage II is defined by recurrent or persistent epithelial defects (PED) without stromal involvement. The PED is usually oval in shape and its margins are characteristically smooth and rolled due to impaired epithelial healing. Descemet's folds and anterior chamber inflammation may be observed. • • Stage III is characterized by stromal involvement leading to corneal ulcer, melting, and perforation. • Congenital Orbital Anomalies

question: Why do nanophthalmic eyes have increased complications in the immediate post- operative period after cataract surgery?

options.A: deep anterior chamber leads to endothelial damage
options.B: zonular laxity leads to vitreous loss
options.C: higher incidence of posterior polar cataracts leads to vitreous loss
options.D: inelastic sclera leads to choroidal detachments

explanation: Nanophthalmos describes an abnormally small eye that has normal internal organization. This condition contrasts with microphthalmos which is a small, disorganized eye. Patients with nanophthalmos have high hyperopia (e.g. +7.00-15.00 D), a short axial length (e.g. 15-20 mm), crowded anterior segments, and thick/rigid sclera. These properties lead to constriction of blood flow through scleral vessels and predispose the eye to choroidal detachments and hemorrhages. For intraocular (mainly glaucoma) surgery, many surgeons will create prophylactic draining sclerotomies to minimize choroidal effusion formation. Nanophthalmic eyes can also have shallow anterior chambers that can lead to a higher incidence of endothelial damage. Extra: Nanophthalmic=Normal eye. Microphthalmic=missed up eye.

question: Which of the following is TYPICALLY associated with nanophthalmos?
explanation: Nanophthalmos is typically associated with chronic angle closure glaucoma due to anterior chamber crowding. Less commonly, glaucoma from nanophthalmos can be due to elevated episcleral venous pressure with an open angle. Unlike microphthalmos, the internal organization of eyes with nanophthalmos is relatively normal. Hyperopia (e.g. 7-15 diopters), short axial length (e.g. 15-20 mm), and strabismus are all commonly associated with nanophthalmos.

question: An 8-year-old patient is brought in by his mom for an eye exam. She says that his right eye is smaller than the left and has not seen well since birth. On exam, you note that the eye is indeed smaller than the left and there are iris and lens abnormalities. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
explanation: This child presents with a small disorganized globe which is also known as microphthalmos. A fissured tongue is not associated with microphthalmos. Trisomy 13, intellectual disability, and dwarfism are associated with microphthalmos. If the eye was small, but organized normally (e.g. normal lens, cornea, etc), then the correct term would be nanophthalmos. Also a possibility with this patient would be aniridia. These patients can have congenital cataracts. Approximately 75-90% of aniridia patients have an autosomal dominant form that is not associated with systemic abnormalities. Also, ~15% of aniridia patients can have WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability) which can occur sporadically or inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. This latter syndrome is due to a mutation in the PAX6 gene. These patients can also have chronic angle closure glaucoma. This would predispose to a larger eye if glaucoma developed as an infant.

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of microcornea:

options.B: autosomal recessive inheritance is most common
options.D: open angle glaucoma occurs 5% of the time

explanation: Microcornea is a condition characterized by a clear cornea of normal thickness, but whose horizontal diameter is less than 10 mm. Individuals with microcornea are typically hyperopic because their corneas are relatively flat. Because of this flat corneal curvature, these individuals are more prone to angle closure glaucoma. For those patients without angle closure glaucoma, still 20% (not 5%) of them will develop an open-angle glaucoma. It is most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion.

question: A hyperopic Finnish boy is brought to your office by his mother. You notice that his corneas are clear and he is seeing well. You happen to get a corneal topography on him which shows the peripheral cornea to be of the same dioptric power as the adjacent sclera. What is the name of the condition that he most likely has?
explanation: Cornea plana is a flat cornea with a central corneal power of less than 43 diopters. The pathognomonic finding is that the cornea curvature is similar to the adjacent sclera. Corneal plana is a common finding in other ocular abnormalities like sclerocornea and colobomas and can be associated with systemic syndromes like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Most isolated cases occur in Finnish individuals. Both open and chronic-angle closure forms of glaucoma can be found in these patients.

question: A mother brings in her 3-year-old child with the finding seen in the photo above. She states that it was present at birth and has not grown much since. Which of the following statements about the most likely diagnosis is correct?

options.A: it most commonly occurs super temporally
options.B: it induces astigmatism 45 degrees away and should be corrected to reduce amblyopia
options.C: the patient is more likely to have kyphosis
options.D: excisional biopsy may be indicated for this lesion

explanation: This patient has an epibulbar dermoid. It may be associated with Goldenhar syndrome which has dental and skeletal abnormalites, and preauricular skin tags. Vertebral abnormalities include butterfly vertebrae; hemivertebrae, which produces secondary scoliosis; kyphosis; and rib anomalies. These lesions should not be excised as they can extend deep into the cornea. A shave biopsy or superficial lamellar dissection may improve astigmatism. It most commonly occurs inferotemporally (don’t confuse this with dermoid cysts which most commonly occur superotemporally). It generally induces plus cylinder astigmatism 90 degrees away and should be corrected to reduce amblyopia.

question: Which of the following tests is NOT able to distinguish megalocornea from buphthalmos in an infant:
explanation: Biomicroscopy under anesthesia with a hand held slit lamp will show a short vitreous length and deep lens and iris with megalocornea. Congenital glaucoma can also have corneal edema from increased IOP and thus have increased pachymetry measurements. Congenital glaucoma can have curvilinear breaks in Descemet membrane (Haab striae). Ultrasound shows the axial length to be normal with megalocornea and elongated with congenital glaucoma. Per BCSC Pediatrics, visual fields cannot be performed reliably in infants. Megalocornea is a nonprogressive and bilateral corneal disease that is mostly inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern (rarely it can be autosomal recessive). It is defined by histologically-normal corneas having horizontal diameters >13 mm. Megalocornea patients can develop glaucoma but generally never have congenital glaucoma. To differentiate megalocornea patients from those with congenital glaucoma, you should perform careful IOP measurement (normal in megalocornea) and A-scan ultrasound (normal axial length and deep anterior chamber in megalocornea). The deep anterior chambers in patients with this anomaly minimize the chance of angle closure glaucoma. The large cornea is associated with a large anterior chamber and angle. It can be associated with Marfan syndrome. Extra:

question: Which of the following is a characteristic of megalocornea?

options.A: It is frequently associated with chronic mydriasis
options.B: It is most commonly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
options.C: It is defined by corneas greater than 12 mm in horizontal diameter
options.D: It can be associated with Marfan syndrome

explanation: Megalocornea is nonprogressive, bilateral corneal disease that is most commonly inherited in a X-linked recessive pattern. There are some rare reports of inheritance in an autosomal recessive pattern. These corneas are histologically-normal, but have horizontal diameters in the 13.0-16.5 mm range. Some common associated clinical findings include: • Iris translucency • Miosis • Cataract • Ectopia lentis • Mosaic corneal dystrophy • Goniodysgenesis • Glaucoma (but not congenital glaucoma) Systemic associations: • Down syndrome • Marfan syndrome • Alport syndrome • Osteogenesis imperfecta • Dwarfism • Hypertelorism • Mental retardation Again, megalocornea patients can have glaucoma, but not typically congenital glaucoma. To differentiate megalocornea infants from those with buphthalmos from congenital glaucoma, you should perform an A-scan. The axial length is normal in those with megalocornea but increased in those with congenital glaucoma. The A-scan can also delineate the short vitreous length and deep lens/iris position typical of megalocornea.

question: Which of the following are difficult to distinguish from corneal dermoids?
explanation: Corneal keloids are bright white and very similar in appearance to dermoids. Salzmann nodules typically have a translucent appearance. Salzmann nodular degeneration is secondary to hyaline material deposited in Bowman's layer. It is generally thought to be due to chronic irritation of the cornea. It is rarely secondary to contact lens use. Extra: dermoids are dense - opaque salzmann are soft - translucent Disease Entity Figure 1 Corneal keloid with glistening white appearance covering large area of the corneal surface. (Reproduced from the British Journal of Ophthalmology,Risco et al [21] with permission from BMJ Publishing Group Ltd.) A corneal keloid is a benign pearly, gray-white epicorneal lesion (Figure 1) that results from abnormal proliferation of fibrous tissue and accumulation of disorganized collagen fibrils and glycoprotein, with characteristic hyperplasia of the corneal epithelium and disruption of Bowman's layer.[1] It can develop after ocular trauma or infection, or can arise congenitally and/or idiopathically. Bilateral cases of corneal keloids are typically associated with congenital disorders including Lowe Syndrome and Rubenstein-Taybi Syndrome

question: Which of the following syndromes or conditions has been reported to be associated with corneal keloids?
explanation: Corneal keloids are rare "chalky white" lesions that are most commonly described after corneal trauma or perforation. They are thought to be due to a vigorous fibrotic response after trauma. They can closely resemble corneal dermoids. In contrast to dermoids, corneal keloids have a more glistening and jellylike quality. Definitive diagnosis can be made with an excisional biopsy. Congenital corneal keloids have been reported to be associated with certain congenital syndromes, such as Lowe syndrome, the ACL syndrome (acromegaly, cutis gyrata, cornea leukoma), and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome. Other associated ocular findings include cataracts, aniridia, and glaucoma. Lowe syndrome importantly also has a high risk of congenital cataracts (~100%) and glaucoma (~50%), ...

question: You are examining a 3 year old patient with the above findings. You are also told that there is a strong family history of breast cancer. Which of the following statements about the condition seen in the photo is true?
explanation: This patient has Ataxia-Telangiectasia (Louis-Barr syndrome). This is an autosomal recessive condition. By age two, these patients develop truncal ataxia followed by dysarthria, dystonia, and choreoathetosis. They are severely physically disabled by age 10. One of the earliest signs in the entire body is the impaired ability to initiate saccades. Teleangiestasias develop between ages 3 to 5. These patients are also more senstive to sunlight, hypoplasia of the thymus, and decreased levels of IgG. This leads to a high prevelance of bacterial associated respiratory death in childhood. The gene defective is called ATM (Ataxia-Telangiectasia Mutated gene). The normal gene is involved in repair of DNA and tumor suppression. The BRCA1 gene is influenced by the gene product. Heterozygous female carriers have a 7x increased risk of breast cancer and may account for 10% of all breast cancers in the U.S. AT patients also have an increased risk of T-cell leukemias Conj Telangiectasia DDx "SOFA" = Sickle cell, OWR, Fabry's, AT

question: You are seeing a patient that you suspect has Ataxia-Telangiectasia (Louis-Barr syndrome). What family history could you elicit from this patient?
explanation: The gene defective is called ATM (Ataxia-Telangiectasia Mutated gene). The normal gene is involved in repair of DNA and tumor suppression. The BRCA1 gene is influenced by the gene product. Heterozygous female carriers have a 7x increased risk of breast cancer and may account for 10% of all breast cancers in the U.S. AT patients also have an increased risk of T-cell leukemias.

question: Which of the following statements about hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler- Weber-Rendu disease) is true?

options.A: it is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern
options.B: it typically manifests in early childhood

explanation: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Rendu-Osler-Weber disease) is generally inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. These patients have telangiectasias of the conjunctiva, nasopharynx, GI tract, brain, and elsewhere. Patients generally do not have bleeding from these abnormal vessels until adulthood. These fragile vessels in the conjunctiva can bleed with minimal eye rubbing. Patients may also have abnormal bleeding from blowing their nose or notice blood in their stool. They may also demonstrate an iron-deficiency anemia on normal blood work.

question: You are called to the neonatal ICU to examine an unusually appearing newborn. The nurse who called the consult says that the newborn was born without eyes. On exam, you note fusion of the eyelids. You then perform an ultrasound and note there is indeed incomplete globe formation. Which of the following would be your diagnosis?
explanation: Cryptophthalmos is a partial or complete failure of the eye to form. Pseudocryptophthalmos occurs when the eyelids fail to separate and gives the appearance of the eye not forming. Anklyoblepharon is when part or all of the eyelid margin fails to separate. "Agenesis oculi" is a made up term. Fraser syndrome associated with cryptophthalmos: think Brendan Fraser in the movie Mummy (crypts).

question: What is the most common syndrome associated with cryptophthalmos?
explanation: The syndrome associated with cryptophthalmos is called Fraser syndrome. In this syndrome, there are malformations in the genitals (e.g. micropenis, cryptorchidism) as well as possible malformations of the nose, ears, larynx and renal system. Fraser syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder that results from mutations in the FRAS1 gene which codes for an extracellular matrix protein. Metabolic Disorders with Corneal Manifestations

question: Which of the following is seen with Bietti crystalline corneoretinal dystrophy?
explanation: Bietti crystalline corneoretinal dystrophy has tapetoretinal dystrophy, corneal crystals, and nyctalopia. It is secondary to a defect in lipid metabolism. The crystals are deposited in the peripheral cornea. Patients have retinal degeneration which leads to the nyctalopia. The differential diagnosis for corneal crystals is the following: macular dystrophy (mucopolysaccharide), granular dystrophy (hyaline), lattice dystrophy (amyloid), Bietti’s and Schnyder’s dystrophies, ciloxan deposits, Strep Viridans causing infectious crystalline keratopathy, cystinosis, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy. Extra: Bietti: crystals at the Border Cystinosis: crystals at the Centre Disease Bietti’s Crystalline Dystrophy (BCD), is a rare autosomal recessive ocular disease that involves yellow-white crystalline lipid deposits in the retina and sometimes cornea, degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and sclerosis of the choroidal vessels. Progression of the disease ultimately results in reduced visual acuity, night blindness, visual field loss, and impaired color vision. Onset of the disease can occur from early teenage years to third decade of life, but can also occur beyond the third decade. As the disease progresses, decreases in peripheral acuity, central acuity or both ultimately results in legal blindness in most patients. Diagnosis Diagnosis of BCD is based on ophthalmic evaluation of numerous small glistening yellow-white retinal crystalline deposits in the retinal with or without crystalline deposits in the cornea, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, pigment clumping, and choroidal vessels sclerosis.[7] The corneal crystals are usually isolated in the subepithelial and anterior stroma of the peripheral cornea (25-33%).[8] CYP4V2 is only moderately expressed in the cornea and the conjunctiva; thus, ocular surface findings are not required for diagnosis

question: Which disorder of amino acid metabolism is characterized by renal impairment and dwarfism in the infantile form and whose corneal changes are exemplified in the photo above?
explanation: Cystinosis is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It is most common in French- speaking Canada. There are three main clinical forms of cystinosis depending on age of presentation: infantile, adolescent, and adult. The infantile form is the most common. Corneal crystals appear as early as 1 year of age and are deposited in the anterior stroma. In patients with severe renal impairment (nephrotic form), patchy depigmentation of the RPE can occur. This generally does not lead to a loss in vision. Tyrosinemia is an autosomal recessive disease secondary to a defect of tyrosine aminotransferase. The diagnosis is made by having an excess level of tyrosine in the blood and urine but a normal phenylalanine level in the blood. These patients present with pseudomembranes. If you ever see a child with recurrent dendrites you should suspect tyrosinemia. These patients don't have true dendrites but rather pseudodendrites meaning that the lesions are not completely devoid of epithelium with distinct margins as they are with an HSV dendrite. These patients are treated by restricting dietary tyrosine and phenylalanine. Doing this leads to a reduction in intellectual disability. Fabry disease is a sphingolipidoses. The three main sphingolipidoses are Fabry disease, multiple sulfatase deficiency, and generalized gangliosidosis. All have corneal verticilata. Fabry disease is inherited in an X-linked pattern and the others in a recessive fashion. Try to remember that Fabry and Hunter and both X-linked. This can be remembered by picturing a "fabulous" Hunter aiming a bow and arrow at a target shaped like an X. Fabry disease can also have renal failure and peripheral neuropathy. The most distinguishing clinical feature is that it has corneal verticilata. Tay-Sachs, another sphingolipidoses, typically has more retinal findings such as a cherry-red spot. question: Three of the following answer choices are disorders of amino acid metabolism. Which of the following is a sphingolipidosis?

question: What is the defective enzyme in Fabry disease:
explanation: Fabry disease is a sphingolipidoses. The three main sphingolipidoses are Fabry disease, multiple sulfatase deficiency, and generalized gangliosidosis. All have corneal verticilata. Fabry disease is inherited in an X-linked pattern and the others in a recessive fashion. Try to remember that Fabry and Hunter are both X-linked. This can be remembered by picturing a "fabulous" Hunter aiming a bow and arrow at a target shaped like an X. Fabry disease can also have renal failure and peripheral neuropathy. The most distinguishing clinical feature is that it has corneal verticilata. Tay-Sachs, another sphingolipidoses, typically has more retinal findings such as a cherry-red spot. Extra: Fabry disease is inherited as an X-linked disease characterized by the following: angiokeratomas of the skin, episodic painful extremities, aneurysmal dilatation of conjunctival vessels and tortuosity of retinal vessels, cornea verticillata, and Spoke-wheel posterior cataracts. Disease Entity Fabry disease is an inability to break down globotriaosylceramide due to a deficiency of α-galactoside A. This results in the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in lysosomes across the entire body. Fabry disease is a type of lysosomal storage disease tht has two recognized forms: classic and atypical. Classic Fabry disease is characterized by dysfunction of the skin, heart, kidney, brain, vascular, ocular, and nervous systems. Atypical Fabry disease usually involves cardiac dysfunction and rarely has any ocular manifestations. Ocular Manifestations Corneal disease: The classic and most common presentation of corneal disease involves the presence of cornea verticillata. Conjunctival disease: Unlike corneal involvement, male and female patients do not differ in terms of conjunctival involvement. Intracellular inclusions that are round in shape have been observed. Retinal disease: The most common finding is retinal vessel tortuosity. Other forms of retinal vessel disease have also been described, including disc edema. Lens disease: Anterior capsular or posterior subcapsular cataracts are the most common manifestations.

question: What is the inheritance pattern of Hunter syndrome?
explanation: Try to remember that Fabry and Hunter syndromes are both X-linked recessive. This can be remembered by imagining a "FABulous HUNTER" aiming a bow and arrow at a target shaped like an "X". The primary ocular manifestation of Hunter syndrome is a pigmentary retinopathy. The ocular signs of Fabry disease are corneal verticillata (see answer image), periorbital edema, posterior spokelike cataracts, comma-shaped conjunctival aneurysms, macular edema, and retinal vessel dilation.

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of the condition seen in the photo?
explanation: This is corneal verticillata. You should know the differential of the most common causes of verticillata: amiodarone (the most common cause), chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, chlorpromazine, subconjunctival gentamicin, ibuprofen, indomethacin, naproxen, and Tamoxifen. An unusual disease with verticillata is Fabry disease. Tangier disease is autosomal recessive disease characterized by an abnormally low serum lipoprotein level. These patients have large orange tonsils; enlarged liver, spleen, and lymph nodes; hypocholesterolemia; abnormal chylomicron remnants; and markedly reduced HDL in the plasma. There is no arcus with this condition, but the corneas do have diffuse opacification and posterior focal infiltrates. Neuropathy leads to lagophthalmos and exposure keratopathy. Fabry disease is a sphingolipidoses. The three main sphingolipidoses are Fabry disease, multiple sulfatase deficiency, and generalized gangliosidosis. All have corneal verticilata. This can be remembered by picturing a "fabulous" Hunter aiming a bow and arrow at a target shaped like an X. Fabry disease can also have renal failure and peripheral neuropathy. The most distinguishing clinical feature is that it has corneal verticillata. Tay-Sachs, another sphingolipidoses, typically has more retinal findings such as a cherry-red spot. Mnemonic: Important FACTS IN identifying whorls in the corneal (corneal verticillata): F: Fabrys A: Amiodarone (m/c) C: chloroquine (hydroxychloroquine)/chlopromazine T: Tamoxifen S: Subconjunctival gentamicin I: Ibuprofen/ Indomethacin N: Naproxen (courtesy of Dr Olga Ceron). Extra: Good mnemonic to remember all the causes of verticillata: "Vernon gently said, "I am --- FABulous!" Vernon = verticillata gently = gentamicin said = NSAIDs I = indomethacin Am = amiodarone --- (hyphen) = hydroxychloroquine and phenothiazine Fabulous = Fabrys disease. Disease Entity Cornea verticillata (also called vortex keratopathy, whorl keratopathy, or Fleischer vortex) describes a whorl-like pattern of golden brown or gray opacities in the corneal epithelium. It is termed cornea verticillata from the Latin noun “verticillus,” meaning "whorl”. Usually asymptomatic, it is caused by the deposition of medications, metabolic substrates, or disease byproducts in the basal epithelial layer of the cornea. Etiology Cornea verticillata is most associated with amiodarone and Fabry disease.[1] It can also be caused by a variety of other medications, the most common of which include:[2] • Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine • Indomethacin • Phenothiazines

question: Which of the following corneal changes is seen with diabetic patients:

options.B: abnormally strong adherence of the epithelium to the stroma

explanation: Diabetes is associated with mild amount of corneal hypoesthesia, poor adherence of the epithelium to the stroma, and a delayed healing time with removal of epithelium at the time of surgery. Thickened posterior nonbanded zone occurs naturally with age.

question: A tall patient presents to your clinic with ectopia lentis in the supratemporal direction. Which of the following consults would be most appropriate to order:
explanation: This patient most likely has Marfan Syndrome. If you were to suspect this, you would want to order a cardiology consult to rule out aortic root dilation and aneurysm. Marfan patients experience superotemporal ectopia lentis. The mechanism of lens subluxation in Marfan's is secondary to abnormal fibrillin. Fibrillin is a component of the lens zonules and the abnormal fibrillin in Marfan's syndrome causes the zonules to be stretched and elongated. 50- 80% of patients with Marfan Syndrome develop ectopia lentis. Another classic condition associated with ectopia lentis is homocystinuria. Patients with homocystinuria are tall and 50% have an intellectual disability. They have inferonasal dislocation of their lenses. In contrast to Marfan's patients, the zonules in homocystinuria patients are brittle and tend to break (not just stretch). These patients are prone to thromoembolic events with general anesthesia. This is very relevant because the co-occurence of intellectual disability and cataracts often necessitates general anesthesia for removal. Dietary restrictions with low methionine and high cysteine as well as coenzyme supplements (pyridoxine or vitamin B6) decrease systemic problems in about 50% of cases.

question: A Slovakian newborn is presented at grand rounds. You are given the information that he has a disorder of amino acid metabolism. He has ocular changes seen in the photo. Which of the following diseases does he likely have:
explanation: This is the classic presentation of alkaptonuria. There is deposition of pigmented material near the medial and lateral rectus muscle insertions. This is secondary to the inability to metabolize tyrosine and phenylalanine. In these patients, their urine turns dark if left standing (i.e. left in a container for a long time). Cystinosis is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It is most common in French-speaking Canadians. There are three main clinical forms of cystinosis depending on age of presentation: infantile, adolescent, and adult. The infantile form is the most common. Corneal crystals appear as early as 1 year of age and are deposited in the anterior stroma. In patients with severe renal impairment (nephrotic form), patchy depigmentation of the RPE can occur. This generally does not lead to a loss in vision. Tyrosinemia is an autosomal recessive disease secondary to a defect of tyrosine aminotransferase. The diagnosis is made by having an excess level of tyrosine in the blood and urine, but a normal phenylalanine level in the blood. These patients present with pseudodendrites. If you ever see a child with recurrent pseudodendrites you should suspect tyrosinemia. These patients do not have true dendrites but rather pseudodendrites meaning that the lesions are not completely devoid of epithelium with distinct margins as they are with a HSV dendrite. These patients are treated by restricting dietary tyrosine and phenylalanine. Doing this leads to a reduction in intellectual disability. Fabry disease is a sphingolipidoses. question: Which of the following is a characteristic of tyrosinemia:
explanation: Tyrosinemia is an autosomal recessive disease secondary to a defect of tyrosine aminotransferase. The diagnosis is made by having an excess level of tyrosine in the blood and urine but a normal phenylalanine level in the blood. These patients present with pseudodendrites. If you ever see a child with recurrent dendrites you should suspect tyrosinemia. These children may have been misdiagnosed as having recurrent HSV keratitis. These patients don't have true dendrites (which is why answer choice B is incorrect) but rather pseudodendrites meaning that the lesions are not completely devoid of epithelium with distinct margins as they are with an HSV dendrite. question: Which degeneration has brownish-golden circular deposits in the superficial stroma that are secondary to age and UV exposure?
explanation: Also known as Labrador keratopathy, it is generally bilateral and located within the interpalpebral fissure. Histopathologically, there is elastotic degeneration that occurs with UV radiation exposure. Treatment is generally with lubrication. It does not generally affect vision to a significant degree.

question: Which of the following ichthyosis disorders is most commonly associated with corneal opacities?

question: A 29-year-old male patient with a history of soft contact lens wear is referred for evaluation and treatment of ten days of cloudy vision, photophobia, pain and redness in the right eye.  He reports he had eye irritation approximately two weeks ago and sought treatment four days later.  He was initially treated with fortified vancomycin and tobramycin every 2 hours, which failed to significantly improve his symptoms.  He has not worn his contact lenses since the initial symptoms started.  Slit-lamp photograph of the right eye is shown above. Which of the following treatment options represents a reasonable strategy at this time?

options.A: Obtain cultures and change to topical fortified ceftazidime every 1 hour
options.B: Obtain cultures, continue topical fortified tobramycin every 1 hour and add topical moxifloxacin every 1 hour
options.C: Obtain cultures, continue topical fortified tobramycin every 1 hour and add topical steroids twice daily
options.D: Obtain cultures, initiate treatment with chlorhexidine 0.02% and propamidine every 1 hour

explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis (AK) is a severe, vision-threatening infection that unfortunately is quite common in contact lens wearers, especially if there an exposure to fresh-water (such as swimming in a lake with contact lenses on). Acanthamoebae are ubiquitous protoza that are highly resistant to eradication. The organism exists as either an active, motile trophozoite or an extremely hardy, dormant double-walled cyst state. The organism can convert between these two states, often converting into the cyst state when under duress. AK is likely the end result of corneal microtrauma induced by contact lens wear since the amoeba is only capable of infection when the corneal epithelium integrity has been compromised. AK presents with the classic symptoms of infectious keratitis, but often there is a protracted clinical course and a history of failed therapy with classical topical antibiotics. In some cases, an obvious source of infection can be identified (such as swimming with contact lenses on, using home made saline solution, showering with contact lenses on, etc.), but contact lens wear may be the sole risk factor. Examination early in the disease state may reveal non-specific findings such as punctate epithelial erosions, irregular epithelium (which can look like a dendrite) and mild conjunctival injection. As the infection progresses, a classic "ring infiltrate" may develop along with varying amounts of anterior chamber reaction. Patients often have significant pain secondary to radial perineuritis. The infection may cause progressive corneal thinning and even perforation. Diagnosing AK can be challenging since it can mimic bacterial (eg, Pseudomonas) and/or viral (eg, herpetic) infections which are also common in contact lens wearers. Options for diagnosing AK include: • Visualization with in-vivo confocal microscopy • Culturing the amoeba in non-nutrient agar with E.coli overlay or charcoal yeast agar • Corneal scraping to preserve the cells with a cytology fixative • Corneal scraping to stain the cells with acridine Orange, calcofluour white, periodic acid-Schiff, Wright-Giemsa or Wheatly trichrome stains • corneal biopsy with visualization performed by a skilled ophthalmic pathologist Given that the patient has not responded to treatment with a fortified antibiotics, it would be reasonable to entertain the diagnosis of AK and proceed with treatment. Changing to fortified ceftazidime (choice A) would not yield much additional benefit given that the patient has already been on fortified tobramycin. Both ceftazidime and tobramycin are better at covering gram negative organisms. Similarly, adding topical moxifloxacin (choice B) would also yield very little benefit given that they are already taking Vancomycin. Adding topical steroids (choice C) would be a very unwise decision especially given that we do not know the causative organism at this time. Therefore, treatment for AK would be the most appropriate course of action at this time. (In real life, one may consider therapy with fortified vancomycin and fortified tobramycin at this time as well, but that is not listed as one of the answer choices) While treatment strategies for AK vary, the choice listed above involves using chlorhexidine with a diamidine. Oral itraconaole/ketoconazole may also be added. PHMB may also be considered, as it has been shown that when used in combination, PHMB can kill both the trophozoite and cyst without significant toxicity to the corneal epithelium.

question: A patient presents with severe ocular pain and a linear epitheliopathy of the right eye.  His past ocular history is only significant for contact lens wear.  Gram stain and confocal microscopy show cysts within the corneal stroma.  Which of the following would be the best choice for initial treatment?
explanation: This question implies that the patient has Acanthamoeba keratitis. One of the hallmark characteristics of this infection is severe eye pain that is out of proportion to the clinical appearance of the cornea. Acanthamoeba keratitis typically begins as an epitheliopathy with or without pseudodendrites and perineural infiltrates. The presence of perineural infiltrates is virtually pathognomonic for Acanthamoeba. The often-seen-on-tests ring infiltrate is actually a late-stage manifestation of Acanthamoeba. Although the trophozoites of Acanthamoeba are highly sensitive to a wide variety of chemotherapeutic substances, the cyst form is highly resistant to most forms of therapy. Effective treatment of Acanthamoeba keratitis requires the agent to be cysticidal. Currently, the diamidines and biguanides are the most effective antiamoebics available. The biguanides that are typically used are PHMB 0.02% and chlorhexidine 0.02% (not 0.01%), of which PHMB is more commonly used. The diamidines include propamidine isethionate 0.1% and hexamidine 0.1%. This author prefers the use of monotherapy with PHMB since combination therapy has not proven superior to PHMB alone and due to corneal toxicity concerns of multi-therapy. Paromomycin 0.5% is an aminoglycoside antibiotic that, like neomycin, is effective against the trophozoite form of Acanthamoeba, but is ineffective against the cyst form. Therefore, it should not be used in the treatment of Acanthamoeba keratitis. Corticosteroids should be used with caution because if used too early they can induce cyst formation and worsen clinical outcomes.

question: Which of the following clinical signs or symptoms is not generally seen with Acanthamoeba keratitis?
explanation: All of the other answer options are common with Acanthamoeba. These infections are generally very painful on presentation because they invade corneal nerves.

question: A patient presents with a discrete inferior marginal anterior corneal infiltrate in the right eye. For the most common cause of this condition, which of the following is true?

options.A: The overlying epithelium is generally absent (epithelial defect)
options.B: It represents a direct infectious process that is best treated with scraping and an antibiotic
options.C: It represents a secondary immunologic component
options.D: It is generally associated with Streptococcus blepharitis

explanation: Discrete inferior infiltrates in the anterior peripheral stroma are most commonly secondary to Staphylococcal marginal keratitis. According to some textbooks (e.g. Krachmer's Cornea), these infiltrates are most likely a type III hypersensitivity reaction (they are not a direct infectious process). However, recent editions of the BCSC have stated that it represents a type IV reaction. In any case, reaction to Staphylococcal antigens (e.g. exotoxins, cell wall proteins) is thought to be the inciting stimulus. Diagnostic scraping is not necessary and could actually lead to a direct corneal infection. The marginal keratitis is best treated with antibiotics aimed at the underlying staphylococcus infection and mild steroids to reduce the inflammatory component Extra: Etiology and pathophysiology The vast majority of patients with marginal keratitis have symptomatic Staphylococcal blepharitis/conjunctivitis, or asymptomatic Staphylococcal colonization of the eyelid.[1] Marginal keratitis is thought to be the product of an inflammatory reaction against staphylococcal antigens (rather than a direct staphylococcal infection of the cornea). The presence of bacterial antigens in the peripheral area of the cornea possibly triggers a type III hypersensitivity reaction, in which immunocomplexes are formed and deposited in the peripheral corneal stroma Physical examination The disease usually begins with the formation of one or more stromal infiltrates in the peripheral cornea, typically in the points of intersection between the eyelid margin and the limbus (i.e. 2, 4, 8, and 10 o’clock positions). These infiltrates are almost always located 1-2mm parallel to the limbus,

question: Ophthalmomyiasis refers to proliferation of what organisms within ocular tissues?
explanation: The term myiasis refers to infestation of tissue by fly maggots and ophthalmomyiasis refers to infestation of ocular structures by fly maggots. While not a concern in your average refractive surgery practice, it is not rare in developing world conditions with poor sanitation. Maggots can gain entry to the eye directly through an unhealthy and susceptible ocular surface or may travel through the blood stream to enter the eye. Tapeworms can affect vision by affecting the visual pathways in the brain in cysticercosis and more rarely other tape worms can settle in virtually any portion of the eye resulting in severe inflammation. Leishmania is a protozoan parasite spread through the bite of sandflies and can affect internal organs or the skin depending on the type. In regards to ophthalmology, Leishmania can cause severe granulomatous inflammation of the eyelids. Extra:

question: A 70-year-old man presents to you for a 3rd opinion regarding his chronically- irritated eyes.  He states that he has been diagnosed with "anterior blepharitis", but that he has found minimal relief with warm compresses, lid scrubs with baby shampoo, and erythromycin ointment.  His ocular exam is significant for erythema of the lid margins, cylindrical dandruff, madarosis, and meibomian gland dysfunction.  You examine some of the eyelashes under the microscope (see video above).  Which of the following most likely would improve this patient's chronic condition?

options.D: tea tree oil to eyelid margins

explanation: The microscope photo is showing a typical Demodex mite, which is the most common parasite found on the human skin. In fact, almost all individuals will be colonized by this mite by 70 years old. There are two Demodex species that colonize humans: D. folliculorum and D. brevis. D. folliculorum typically is associated with "anterior blepharitis" (i.e. infestation of the lashes and follicles) while D. brevis is characteristically associated with "posterior blepharitis" (i.e. infestation of the meibomian glands). You should start to suspect Demodex-associated blepharitis in the following situations: • When a patient's blepharitis is recalcitrant to conventional treatments • Cylindrical dandruff is present at the base of the lashes • When there is madarosis or recurrent trichiasis. The classic treatment for Demodex-associated blepharitis is with tea tree oil (TTO) (e.g. daily scrub with 50% TTO and/or lid massage with 5% TTO ointment). One of the commercial formulations of TTO is marketed as Cliradex®. Other treatment options are oral ivermectin or oral metronidazole.

question: A patient presents with a granulomatous conjunctivitis and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy. What was the most likely source of the infection?
explanation: Granulomatous conjunctivitis with regional lymphadenopathy defines Parinaud's ocularglandular syndrome. This rare syndrome presents with a unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis that develops approximately 1 week after exposure to a causative microorganism. In addition, the preauricular and/or the submandibular lymph nodes become tender and may be accompanied by constitutional symptoms (e.g. fever, malaise, headache). The majority of cases are caused by Cat-scratch disease which describes how the primary causative microorganism, Bartonella henselae is transmitted to humans. In reality, the affected individual usually cannot recall being scratched by a cat, but instead is exposed to the cat's saliva through licking. Other causes of Parinaud's includes tularemia (transmitted by rabbits), sporotrichosis, tuberculosis, and syphillis. The "gold-standard" treatment of Parinaud's is not agreed upon. Various antibiotic regimens have been successful (e.g. azithromycin, doxycycline). Extra:

question: A 21 year old patient presents to the Tulane emergency room with severe eye pain.  On exam, there are superficial feathery anterior stromal infiltrates and also anterior white raised colonies.  He is suspected to have a fungal keratitis with both Aspergillus and Candida.  What would be the best initial treatment?
explanation: Trauma with plant or vegetable matter, contact lens wear, prior corneal surgery (e.g. PKP and RK), chronic keratitis, and topical steroids increase the risk for fungal keratitis. Infection with Candida is more common in immunocompromised hosts and corneas with chronic epithelial defects. Pain with fungal ulcers is generally out of proportion to clinical signs (e.g. corneal edema). Filamentous fungal keratitis (e.g. Aspergillus and Fusarium) presents as a gray- white infiltrate with a "feathery" margin. Multifocal or satellite lesions may occur. Anterior lesion may elevate the surface of the cornea and have a rough, dry, or gritty appearance. Candida is the most common cause of yeast keratitis. It presents with anterior raised colonies. It most frequently remains superficial. Culture with blood, Sabouraud, and brain-heart infusion agars are the preferred culturing method. Confocal microscopy can identify fungal cysts and filaments. Natamycin 5% is the preferred initial treatment for filamentous fungus including Fusarium infections. The majority of fungal infections in the United States occur in the Southern U.S. and are secondary to Fusarium. This patient is located in New Orleans. So, if you are in the Southern U.S. and suspect a purely filamentary fungal infection, it is best to use natamycin 5% until the cultures are back. The other convenient thing about natamycin 5% is that it is commercially produced which means that when you send the patient to the pharmacy to pick it up, they will actually have it. Amphotericin B is a good treatment for both the filamentary Aspergillus fungal infection and those caused by the yeast Candida fungal keratitis. It is used to treat corneal ulcers caused by Candida and Aspergillus. Patients have to be sent to a compounding pharmacy for this medication. For this question, Amphotericin B is a good choice because it covers both of the suspected organisms. A newer anti-fungal that has excellent antifungal properties is voriconazole. It can be given both topically as a 1% concentration and orally. The oral form could be considered with deep corneal infections or in cases with progession to endophthalmitis. One factor that limits its use is that it is typically more expensive and also needs to be compounded. Recent studies suggest that it may be inferior to natamycin for Fusarium solani infections. For this question, answer choice D is not a good option because of the potential side effects of oral voriconazole (e.g. liver toxicity). Topical 1% voriconazole would be an acceptable answer choice. Therapeutic corneal transplant without prior eradication of the fungus has a poor prognosis with frequent recurrence of the infection in the graft. Extra: FUsarium= Natamycin, Candida Aspergillus= AMPhotericin B (FUN CAAMP)

question: Which of the following fungal infections is more commonly associated with a fulminant keratitis?
explanation: The BCSC Cornea book specifically mentions the following filamentous fungi: • Fusarium spp (e.g. F. solani and F. oxysporum). • Aspergillus • Curvularia • Paecilomyces • Phialophora Of these, Fusarium species are more commonly associated with a fulminant keratitis. In general, filamentous fungi are most commonly the causative organism for fungal keratitis associated with trauma and contact lens wear. In contrast, yeast (e.g. Candida spp) are most frequently the causative organism in patients with ocular surface disease (e.g. severe dry eye, post-penetrating keratoplasty). Lastly, the most common causes of fungal keratitis in the United States are trauma and contact lens wear. However, trauma is overwhelmingly the most common cause of fungal keratitis in developing countries since the rate of contact lens wear is much lower in the developing world. Extra: Fusarium = fulminant

question: A contact lens wearing patient from Louisiana presents with a fungal keratitis. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: Natamycin 5% is used for Fusarium infections. The majority of fungal infections in the United States occur in the Southern U.S. and are secondary to Fusarium. So, if you are in the Southern U.S. and suspect a fungal infection, it is best to use Natamycin 5% until the cultures are back. The other convenient thing about Natamycin 5% is that it is commercially produced which means that when you send the patient to the pharmacy to pick it up, they will actually have it. Amphotericin B is used to treat Candida and Aspergillus. Patients have to be sent to a compounding pharmacy for this medication. A new anti-fungal that has excellent antifungal properties is voriconazole. It can be given both topically and orally. One factor that limits its use is its extreme expense.

question: Which of the following culture media is most optimal for isolating fungi?
explanation: Sabouraud's agar is best for fungi. Lowenstein-Jensen is best for isolating mycobacteria. Aerobic bacteria can be cultured with blood agar, chocolate agar, and thioglycollate broth. Anaerobic bacteria are ideally cultured with thioglycollate broth. Thayer-Martin agar is best for Neisseria. Acanthamoeba is best cultured with nonnutrient agar with E. coli overlay. Blood and chocolate agars are good overall culture plates. Middlebrook agar grows out non-tuberculous mycobacteria (seen after LASIK).
