question: Which of the following statements best describes the comparative efficacy of topical natamycin versus topical voriconazole in the treatment of fungal keratitis according to the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (aka MUTT I)?

options.A: Natamycin treatment was associated with significantly better clinical outcomes than voriconazole
options.B: Voriconazole treatment was associated with significantly better clinical outcomes than natamycion
options.C: There was no statistically significant difference between natamycin and voriconazole
options.D: Fusarium cases fared better with voriconazole compared to natamycin

explanation: The Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (aka MUTT I) was a randomized, controlled, double- blind trial comparing the efficacy of topical natamycin 5% versus topical voriconazole 1%. All enrolled participants had smear-positive fungal corneal ulcers and baseline visual acuity of 20/40 to 20/400. These participants were enrolled at Aravind Eye Care Hospitals in three different cities in India. The primary outcome was best spectacle-corrected visual acuity (BSCVA) 3 months after enrollment. The MUTT found that the natamycin-treated group did 1.8 lines better than the voriconazole-treated group at 3 months (mean BSCVA was 0.39 logMAR and 0.57 logMAR in the natamycin- and voriconazole-treated groups respectively). Subgroup analysis found that this efficacy difference was mainly for Fusarium cases where the natamycin-treated group did 4.1 lines better than the voriconazole-treated group. There was no difference in adjusted BSCVA between the two groups in non-Fusarium cases. Other interesting findings from this trial: • Natamycin-treated cases were significantly less likely to be culture-positive (<10% cases) after 6 days of treatment in contrast to voriconazole-treated cases (>50%). • Reepithelialization time and 3-month infiltrate or scar size were not significantly different between the two groups. A sister study, the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (MUTT II), was a similarly-designed trial except that it was comparing the effectiveness of oral voriconazole versus placebo (in addition to topical antifungals). The primary outcome examined was the rate of corneal perforation or the need for therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty. The MUTT II found no benefit of adding oral voriconazole to topical antifungals for this primary outcome variable. SUMMARY: • MUTT I -- topical natamycin 5% is superior to topical voriconazole 1% (most of this effect was from Fusarium cases) o MUTT II -- there is no benefit of adding oral voriconazole (and higher adverse events) on top of topical anti-fungals.

question: A 35-year-old presents with a severe, central corneal ulcer of the right eye.  His history is significant for being a farmer who works in the fields every day.  You perform a Gram stain and filamentous fungal elements are seen.  You start the patient on natamycin 5% q1hour and are contemplating your management options. According to the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial II (i.e. MUTT II), what would be the most appropriate management of this patient?

options.A: In addition to topical natamycin 5%, the patient should be started on oral voriconazole
options.B: The patient should be treated with topical anti-fungals only
options.C: The patient should be switched from natamycin 5% to voriconazole 1% q1hour
options.D: In addition to topical natamycin 5%, the patient should be started on topical voriconazole 1% q1hour

explanation: The Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (aka MUTT II), was a placebo-controlled, randomized trial that was conducted in several centers in India and Nepal. Its main objective was to compare the effectiveness of oral voriconazole versus placebo (all patients received topical antifungals). The primary outcome examined was the rate of corneal perforation or the need for therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty. The MUTT II found no benefit of adding oral voriconazole to topical antifungals for this primary outcome variable. Other interesting results of the MUTT II: • Mean 3-month visual acuity was no different in the placebo vs. oral voriconazole groups. • Mean 3-week and 3-month infiltrate and/or scar size was similar between the two groups. • No difference in re-epithelialization rates between the two groups. • Higher rate of adverse events in the oral voriconazole group (P=0.001). These adverse events included: elevated liver function tests and visual hallucinations. A sister study, the Mycotic Ulcer Treatment Trial (aka MUTT I) was a randomized, controlled, double-blind trial comparing the efficacy of topical natamycin 5% versus topical voriconazole 1%. All enrolled participants had smear-positive fungal corneal ulcers and baseline visual acuity of 20/40 to 20/400. These participants were enrolled at Aravind Eye Care Hospitals in three different cities in India. The primary outcome was best spectacle-corrected visual acuity (BSCVA) 3 months after enrollment. The MUTT found that the natamycin-treated group did 1.8 lines better than the voriconazole-treated group at 3 months (mean BSCVA was 0.39 logMAR and 0.57 logMAR in the natamycin- and voriconazole-treated groups respectively). Subgroup analysis found that this efficacy difference was mainly for Fusarium cases where the natamycin-treated group did 4.1 lines better than the voriconazole-treated group. There was no difference in adjusted BSCVA between the two groups in non-Fusarium cases. Other interesting findings from this trial: • Natamycin-treated cases were significantly less likely to be culture-positive (<10% cases) after 6 days of treatment in contrast to voriconazole-treated cases (>50%). • Reepithelialization time and 3-month infiltrate or scar size were not significantly different between the two groups. SUMMARY: • MUTT I -- topical natamycin 5% is superior to topical voriconazole 1% (most of this effect was from Fusarium cases) • MUTT II -- there is no benefit of adding oral voriconazole (and higher adverse events) on top of topical anti-fungals.

question: What is the leading risk factor for the development of fungal keratitis?
explanation: While all of the other choices increase the risk for fungal keratitis, trauma is the most common risk factor.

question: Which of the following is a nonseptate fungus?
explanation: Nonseptate filamentous fungi include Mucor, Absidia, and Rhizopus. These fungi can cause life- threatening infections ("mucormycosis") of the paranasal sinuses, brain, and orbit, typically in immunocompromised patients. A typical clinical scenario is a poorly-controlled diabetic hospitalized for diabetic ketoacidosis. Other predisposing conditions include renal failure and gastroenteritis. These patients present with an orbital cellulitis with early visual loss from orbital apex syndrome. Another often-tested sign is seeing black eschar-like crusting in the nose or on the hard palate. Septate fungi include Fusarium, Aspergillus, and Curvularia. A nice mnemonic is: "F.A.C.t.S"

question: A 23-year-old man presents to your clinic with severely-decreased vision and severe pain in the left eye. His only past ocular history is soft contact lens wear. What is the most likely microorganism that caused the ocular condition seen in this photo?
explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa corneal infections typically result in fulminant corneal ulcers with a "soupy" appearance. These highly-destructive ulcers usually have an explosive onset and can perforate the cornea within a day. This gram negative rod is the most common cause of bacterial keratitis in soft contact lens wearers. Frequently, patients with these ulcers require initial hospitalization with around-the-clock fortified antibiotics. Extra: Disease Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative rod. It is an opportunistic human pathogen, known to cause a variety of infectious diseases. In the eye, P. aeruginosa is a common cause of bacterial keratitis, particularly in contact lens wearers. It is known to be particularly virulent, with pseudomonas keratitis being more difficult to treat and have worse prognosis than other forms of bacterial keratitis. P. aeruginosa secretes proteases that can cause liquefactive necrosis of the cornea, leading to rapid corneal weakening and perforation. Diagnosis and treatment All cases of suspected pseudomonas keratitis should be scraped and cultured. Empiric broad spectrum antibiotics should be initiated for infectious keratitis. Treatment regimens for pseudomonas keratitis are variable and include monotherapy or combination therapy with a topical fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, cephalosporins, , carbapenems and chloramphenicol

question: Which of the following is LEAST ideal for obtaining bacterial cultures?
explanation: Bacterial cultures are best obtained with a platinum Kimura spatula (because it heats and cools rapidly), metal blade, calcium alginate, or Dacron swab. Cotton-tipped swabs are not ideal since cotton can inhibit growth. Typically, the corneal scrapings are used to create rows of "C"s in the culture plate (see answer image). Each row should be from a different sample after heating the spatula. The culture is considered positive when at least two rows grow the bacteria. The "C"s help the microbiologist identify the specimen as being sampled from the "Cornea". Viral cultures are best obtained by using a Dacron swab to swab the specimen, dipping the swab in chilled viral transport media, and then discarding the swab. The calcium in a calcium alginate swab and the wood shaft from a cotton swab can inhibit viral recovery. Lowenstein-Jensen is used to culture mycobacteria and Nocardia species. Aerobic bacteria can be cultured with blood agar, chocolate agar, and thioglycolate broth. Chocolate agar specifically grows Haemophilus species and Neisseria gonorrhoeae well. Anaerobic bacteria are ideally cultured with thioglycolate broth. Thayer-Martin agar is best for Neisseria species. Acanthamoeba is best cultured with nonnutrient agar with E. coli overlay. Sabouraud's agar is best for fungi.

question: A 27-year-old man presents with 12 hours of right eye pain and purulent discharge as shown above.  He has had 4 new sexual partners in the past two months.  Which of the following is the most likely finding on the Gram stain of the discharge?
explanation: This patient has gonococcal conjunctivitis due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a Gram-negative diplococcus (answer B). Gonococcal conjunctivitis is characterized by its hyperacute nature, overwhelming purulent discharge, and N. gonorrhaoeae’s ability to invade intact corneal epithelium. N. gonorrhoeae can induce keratolysis and lead to corneal perforation without prompt treatment. As N. gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted infection, patients with a history of numerous sexual partners are at higher risk for contracting the infection. Treatment of gonococcal conjunctivitis is 1g intramuscular ceftriaxone along with co-treatment of suspected chlamydia with 1g oral azithromycin. In cases with corneal involvement, hospitalization and treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone 1g daily is recommended. Topical fluoroquinolone drops and frequent saline irrigation should be utilized until the discharge resolves. All sexual partners should receive treatment for gonorrhea and chlamydia as well.

question: Which of the following would be a suitable treatment for gonococcal conjunctivitis in an adult?
explanation: The treatment of gonococcal conjunctivitis is high yield. The key here is to remember that gonococcal conjunctivitis is a systemic disease requiring systemic treatment. The mainstay of treatment is a one time dose of 1 gram of intramuscular (IM) ceftriaxone. In penicillin-allergic patients, a one time dose of IM spectinomycin or 5-7 days of oral fluoroquinolones can be used. Additional topical medications can be used along with frequent irrigation of the eye with normal saline in cases of severe conjunctivitis or corneal involvement. Due to the high rate of co-infection with Chlamydia, it is generally suggested that patients with gonococcal conjunctivitis also be treated for Chlamydia. The best treatment options for Chlamydia are doxycycline or azithromycin. This question does not give an answer choice to treat both gonococcal conjunctivitis and Chlamydia so choose the best option (to treat just the gonococcal conjunctivitis in this case).

question: A 24-year-old man presents with 6 hours of discharge and blurry vision in the right eye.  He denies any recent fevers, chills, or other systemic symptoms.  He states that his eye was normal prior to onset of symptoms this morning.  Right eye exam is significant for copious purulent discharge, 3+ diffuse conjunctival injection and 3+ conjunctival papillae.  The cornea is clear without infiltrates or epithelial defects.  Left eye exam is normal.  The patient has a history of an anaphylactic reaction to cephalosporins.  What is the recommended management?
explanation: his patient’s hyperacute onset of conjunctivitis with a papillary reaction and copious mucopurulent discharge is typical for gonococcal conjunctivitis. It is critical to elicit sexual history, which is not provided in this vignette. These patients must be monitored daily until clinical improvement is noted. Corneal involvement can rapidly lead to perforation and any patient with corneal involvement must be admitted to the hospital for treatment. First-line treatment is 1 g IM ceftriaxone for gonococcal conjunctivitis with 1 g po azithromycin being administered as well due to the high rate of co-infection with Chlamydia. Frequent topical fluoroquinolone drops and saline irrigation are also recommended. If corneal involvement is present, 1 g IV ceftriaxone every 12-24 hours while inpatient is recommended. Patients who have an IgE-mediated allergic reaction to cephalosporins (e.g. anaphylaxis, Stevens- Johnson syndrome) may receive gentamicin or gemifloxacin. There should be a low threshold to consult Infectious Disease in these patients or any patient admitted to the hospital with corneal involvement.

question: Which of the following findings are seen in Chlamydia trachoma?

options.A: conjunctival follicles on the lower tarsal conjunctiva leading to an Arlt line
options.B: limbal follicles and their sequelae (Herbert pits)
options.D: vascular pannus most marked on the lateral limbus

explanation: Chlamydia trachoma leads to limbal follicles and their sequelae (i.e. Herbert pits), tarsal conjunctival scarring, and a vascular pannus that is most marked on the superior limbus. Conjunctival follicles are most numerous on the superior tarsus.

question: Which Chlamydia serovars are associated with trachoma?

options.D: serovars M2 A A Here is a summary of the serovars that are associated with the different Chlamydial diseases: • Trachoma:  serovars A-C. • Adult and neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis:  serovars D-K • lymphogranuloma venereum:  L1-L3,

explanation: Some memorable mnemonics: • "trAChoma" --> serovars A-C (Courtesy of Dr Jorges Montes) • "DicK" - which references that adult/neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis are due to sexually transmitted disease

question: What is the difference between a true membrane and a pseudomembrane in regards to the conjunctiva?

options.A: Pseudomembranes are anterior to the basement membrane
options.D: Membrane lead to scarring and entropion

explanation: Classically, it is taught that true membranes are typically very difficult to remove and will result in bleeding if stripped off of the conjunctival surface. In contrast, pseudomembranes usually peel off easily from the conjunctival surface without bleeding. In real clinical practice, since both are signs of severe conjunctival inflammation, both can bleed when peeled off. Situations where true membranes occur include: bacterial conjunctivitis, chemical burns, and ligneous conjunctivitis. Scenarios where pseudomembranes occur include: ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, Steven Johnson syndrome, EKC (epidemic keratoconjunctivitis), and superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis.

question: A 32-year-old personal injury attorney comes to your office with complaints of chronically red and irritated eyes for the past 4 weeks. On exam, you note a prominent follicular reaction mainly involving the lower palpebral conjunctiva as well as a mucopurulent discharge. There are no eyelid lesions and he does not use any medications. Given your presumptive diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.A: erythromycin ointment OU bid for 2 weeks

explanation: This gentleman presents with a chronic follicular conjunctivitis of both eyes. "Chronic" conjunctivitis is defined as lasting more than 3 weeks in duration while "acute" conjunctivitis is 3 weeks or less in duration. The 3 main causes of chronic follicular conjunctivitis are molluscum contagiosum, drug toxicity, and Chlamydia infections. The two types of Chlamydia infections are trachoma and inclusion conjunctivitis. In this case, since the patient does not take any medications (e.g. eyedrops like brimonidine) or has any eyelid findings (e.g. molluscum lesions), he most likely has inclusion conjunctivitis. Inclusion conjunctivitis is the most common ocular chlamydial infection in developed countries. It is considered a sexually-transmitted disease obtained by genital-ocular transmission. Alternatively, it can be contracted through sharing of eye cosmetics (e.g. mascara) or poorly chlorinated swimming pools. It presents with a follicular conjunctivitis preferentially involving the lower palpebral conjunctiva. These follicles are typically larger than the follicles seen in adenoviral conjunctivitis. Like adenoviral, inclusion conjunctivitis can present with subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs), but these tend to be less diffuse and more peripheral. Since inclusion conjunctivitis is a systemic disease, the treatment regimen MUST include oral antibiotics. Common regimens are azithromycin 1 gram (single dose), doxycycline 100 mg bid for 7 days, and erythromycin 500 mg qid for 7 days.

question: Which of the following is a treatment for gonorrhea conjunctivitis:

options.B: topical steroids to slow corneal melt
options.D: treatment for high rate of concurrent HSV

explanation: Gonorrhea conjunctivitis can be treated with IM injection of 1 gram of ceftriaxone, eye lavage every hour, and treatment for the high rate of concurrent chlamydia. Never put steroids on an infectious process! Extra:

question: A 46-year-old man presents to your clinic with complaints of redness and mucus discharge of both eyes for the past 1 months.  On exam, you note a prominent follicular conjunctivitis that equally involves the superior and inferior palpebral conjunctiva.  In addition, you see some mild macropannus of the perilimbal cornea.  His history is significant for working at the local zoo.  Which of the following would be the preferred treatment for this patient?
explanation: his vignette is alluding to the chronic follicular conjunctivitis that can be caused by Chlamydia psittaci which is an organism that can be spread from birds and mammals to humans. "Psittacosis" is also known as "bird fanciers disease" since this organism is transmitted from either the aerosolized fecal matter of birds (e.g. parrots, cockatoos) or their respiratory secretions. The classic presentation of systemic psittacosis is a young or middle-aged adult who presents with an abrupt fever, dry cough, and headache. There are a plethora of other systemic findings that can also occur which will not be detailed here (e.g.hepatomegaly and splenomegaly). The chronic follicular conjunctivitis associated with Chlamydia psittaci can occur without associated systemic symptoms. It is characterized by a follicular conjunctivitis that equally involves the superior and inferior palpebral conjunctiva. This contrasts with trachoma which typically involves the SUPERIOR palpebral conjunctiva and adult inclusion conjunctivitis which typically involves the LOWER palpebral conjunctiva. Remember that neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (i.e. one of the ophthalmia neonatorum diseases) strangely results in a papillary (i.e. not follicular) reaction. Other ocular findings in psittacosis includes possible bulbar follicles, a diffuse punctate epithelial keratitis, and macropannus (i.e. >1 mm). The BCSC lumps infection with Chlamydia psittaci in with Chlamydia trachoma. Common regimens to treat Chlamydia trachoma are azithromycin 1 gram (single dose), doxycycline 100 mg bid for 7 days, and erythromycin 500 mg qid for 7 days. However, recent studies suggest that longer treatment regimens may be needed to treat Chlamydia psittaci. The preferred treatment is usually with an extended course of doxycycline 100 mg po bid. Second-line therapy includes the macrolides such as oral erythromycin or azithromycin. The course of treatment is typically much longer (e.g. >2 months) than for either trachoma or adult inclusion conjunctivitis.

question: Which of the following clinical features of chlamydial conjunctivitis in neonates is TRUE compared to chlamydial conjunctivitis seen in adults?

options.A: Neonates will typically have less mucopurulent discharge compared to adults because their immune systems are less developed
options.B: Infection in neonates has a poor response to topical medications
options.C: Clinical examination of neonates is unlikely to show a follicular response on the conjunctiva
options.D: Giemsa-stained specimens from the conjunctiva of neonates is unlikely to demonstrate intracytoplasmic inclusions

explanation: Per the BCSC Cornea book, there are several distinguishing clinical and laboratory features between chlamydial conjunctivitis in neonates and adults. Among them, there is no follicular response in newborns because lymphoid tissue becomes evident in the human conjunctiva only after a few weeks-to-months of life. In addition, neonates will have a greater amount of mucopurulent discharge. Intracytoplasmic inclusions are seen in a greater percentage of conjunctival specimens from newborns as well. Finally, chlamydial conjunctivitis in neonates is more likely to have a favorable response to topical medications. Nevertheless, both oral and topical treatment is the preferred treatment protocol (e.g. systemic erythromycin and topical erythromycin/sulfacetamide).

question: Which of the following bacteria is particularly associated with a chronic angular blepharoconjunctivitis (i.e. occurring at the lateral canthal angle)?
explanation: The most common cause of chronic blepharoconjunctivitis is Staphylococcus aureus. But Moraxella lacunata is specifically associated with a chronic angular blepharoconjunctivitis. This condition is characterized by crusting and ulceration of the skin in the lateral canthal angle. It can also produce a papillary or follicular reaction of the tarsal conjunctiva.

question: Mycobacteria can be cultured with:
explanation: Aerobic bacteria can be cultured with blood agar, chocolate agar, and thioglycollate broth. Anaerobic bacteria are ideally cultured with thioglycollate broth. Thayer-Martin agar is best for Neisseria. Lowenstein-Jensen is best for myobacteria. Acanthamoeba is best cultured with Nonnutrient agar with E Coli overlay. Sabouraud's agar is best for fungus. Blood and chocolate agars are good overall culture plates. Middlebrook agar grows out non-tuberculous mycobacteria (seen after LASIK).

question: For corneal scrapings, anaerobic bacteria are cultured ideally with which media?
A 64-year-old pseudophakic patient comes in with a 4-month history of mild iritis, vitritis, and a cloudy posterior capsule.  What diagnosis should come to mind?
explanation: This patient presents with delayed-onset (chronic) endophthalmitis. This is typically caused by Propionibacterium acnes. Other ocular signs include granulomatous ("mutton-fat") keratic precipitates, a small hypopyon, and a mild vitritis. These patients typically respond to topical steroids and have the appearance of posterior capsular opacity. Cultures and intravitreal antibiotic are indicated. If this does not cure the situation, vitrectomy with partial capsular bag removal can be performed. Some patients require their entire capsular bag and intraocular lens to be removed.

question: Which of the following microorganisms is classically associated with an explosive endophthalmitis following penetrating trauma to the eye?
explanation: Bacillus are characterized as Gram-positive or Gram-variable rods and are commonly found in soil or other vegetative material. They also are characterized by the production of spores which allows for their survival under adverse environmental conditions. Bacillus cereus is commonly associated with human food poisoning. The classic clinical scenario is someone suffering food poisoning after eating fried rice that has been sitting at room temperature for an extended of time ("fried rice syndrome"). Endophthalmitis caused by Bacillus species is typically explosive in presentation. The typical clinical scenario is post-traumatic endophthalmitis whereby soil is introduced inside a ruptured globe. Factors thought to contribute to this explosiveness are: (1) the species' motile nature; and (2) the different toxins secreted by these species. Bacillus cereus accounts for approximately 25% of cases of post-traumatic endophthalmitis. This organism is sensitive to vancomycin or clindamycin given intravitreally.

question: Which of the following organisms is associated with an acute fulminant endophthalmitis following an open globe injury contaminated with soil?
explanation: Bacillus cereus accounts for ~25% of cases of traumatic endophthalmitis. It is rarely a cause of endophthalmitis in other clinical settings (e.g. post-cataract surgery). Endophthalmitis caused by this organism is extremely aggressive and frequently even results in loss of the eye.

question: Which of the following can be used in the treatment for corneal microsporidiosis?
explanation: According to the BCSC Cornea, Microsporida are protozoa but they have recently been reclassified as fungi. Rarely, they can cause conjunctivitis or epithelial keratitis in immunocompromised individuals, particularly AIDS patients. In immunocompetent patients microsporida can rarely cause stromal keratitis. In immunocompromised patients where the disease is generally more severe, topical fumagillin can be successful in treating the keratoconjunctivitis. Ivermectin is not used in an ophthalmic drop formulation. Oral ivermectin is used to treat many different worm parasites including “river blindness,” or onchocerciasis. Natamycin is a polyene antifungal agent (like amphotericin) often used in topical form for the treatment of fungal keratitis. Polyhexamethylene biguanide is a disinfectant often used to clean swimming pools. Oddly, it is also effective as a topical treatment for Acanthamoeba keratitis.

question: A homeless 28-year-old very thin man presents to your clinic with a 1-month history of right ocular irritation. His past medical history is significant for PCP pneumonia and repeated bouts of oral thrush.  On exam he has mild, diffuse conjunctival injection and chemosis of the right eye.  You obtain a scraping of the conjunctiva which shows small gram-positive spores in the epithelial cells.  Which of the following is the best treatment for this patient?
explanation: This patient is presenting with microsporidiosis. Topical fumagillin is the treatment of choice. The past medical history of PCP pneumonia suggests he has AIDS. Microsporidia most commonly occurs in patients with AIDS or who are severely immunocompromised. These patients often present with conjunctivitis and epithelial keratopathy. Scraping of the conjunctival epithelial cells with the Brown and Hopps stain will reveal small gram-positive spores.

question: A 22-year-old male presents to clinic complaining of itchy eyelids. On exam he has the findings seen in the photo. Which of the following is an accurate recommendation for this patient?

options.B: ointment BID for 5 days to smother the nits
options.C: Bed linen washed and dried at the highest temperature setting (at least 50°C)

explanation: The first photo shows pubic lice. The second photo shows the lice on the eyelashes. The nits' eggs hatch in 10 days. Therefore, the ointment has to be applied for a minimum of 10 days. Mechanical removal and treatment of the sexual partner are also treatments. What is the most common cause of acute dacryoadenitis? A.herpes simplex virus B.varicella zoster virus C.Epstein-Barr virus D.cytomegalovirus A: Acute inflammation of the lacrimal gland is most often secondary to sterile inflammatory disease. The most common viral cause is from Epstein-Barr virus. Extra: Disease Inflammation of the lacrimal gland, either the main or the accessory lacrimal gland, is called dacryoadenitis. Not infrequently, this may be a sign of more sinister pathology underlying the inflammation. Etiology Inflammation may result from infections, most commonly viral, but may also be of bacterial and rarely fungal and parasitic etiology. Other causes of inflammation include autoimmune disorders such as Thyroid Eye Disease, Sjogren's syndrome, IgG4 related disease, etc. The most common infectious etiology for dacryoadenitis is viral, with Epstein-Barr virus being the most common viral cause. Less common viral causes include adenovirus, varicella zoster, herpes simplex, rhinovirus, cytomegalovirus or mumps. Bacterial causes include Staphylococcus aureus, especially methicillin-resistant S. aureus, as well as Streptococcus species. In endemic risk areas, tuberculous infections and abscesses have also been reported. Signs Right-sided dacryoadenitis in a young man. Signs of dacryoadenitis include tenderness, edema, erythema or induration overlying the superolateral orbit, lid ptosis, conjunctival injection with or without chemosis, regional lymphadenopathy, proptosis, limitation of ocular motility and rarely visual loss. Fever and malaise may be present. Management Medical therapy Depending on the severity of the presentation, therapy could include observation and symptomatic treatment for viral dacryoadenitis. Bacterial dacryoadenitis will require systemic broad spectrum antibiotics and, when indicated, abscess drainage. Oral corticosteroids may be considered especially in idiopathic dacryoadenitis. Refractory cases may benefit from orbital radiation or systemic therapy such as rituximab or methotrexate. Biopsy for tissue diagnosis should be considered if concerned for atypical infections or for refractory disease. Surgery Although typically reserved for severe or recurrent cases, a trans-septal or trans-conjunctival biopsy of the lacrimal gland may be of diagnostic value if the etiology is in question

question: What is the most commmon cause of viral dacryoadenitis (i.e. inflammation of the lacrimal gland)?
explanation: Dacryoadentitis is most commonly caused by a sterile inflammatory disease (orbital pseudotumor variant). EBV is the most common cause of viral dacryoadenitis (lacrimal gland inflammation). The multifocal corneal infiltrates are particularly associated with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).

question: A chalazion involves chronic inflammation of which glands?
explanation: A chalazion is a lipogranulomatous inflammation involving either the meibomian or Zeis glands which develops from their obstruction. Histologically, a zonal granulomatous inflammatory response centered around lipid is seen. Please remember that meibomian and Zeis glands are examples of holocrine glands and are located within the tarsus (meibomian) and near the lid margin (Zeis). Other types of glands with some brief facts are: • Lacrimal gland - eccrine gland; located in superotemporal orbit • Krause/Wolfring (accessory lacrimal glands) - eccrine gland; located in fornix • glands of Moll - apocrine gland ("Molly is a sweaty ape"); located near lid Margin • goblet - holocrine gland; conjunctiva and caruncle Disease Entity Chalazion are differentiated from hordeolum (both external and internal); hordeolum result from acute purulent inflammation of eyelid glands. An external hordeolum (stye) involves the eyelash follicles; an internal hordeolum arises from bacterial infection of a meibomian gland. Disease Chalazion is a chronic sterile lipogranuloma residing within eyelid that originates from an obstructed meibomian gland of the tarsal plates.

question: Which of the following antibiotics is most effective for chalazia treatment?
explanation: Chalazia are sterile inflammations. Therefore, antibiotics do not help the process, with the exception of patients having chalazia and rosacea where tetracyclines (doxycycline) and macrolides (erythromycin) work due to their anti-inflammatory properties.

question: Chalazia are generally secondary to infection with which microorganism?
explanation: Chalazia are sterile inflammations. Therefore, antibiotics do not help the process.

question: A patient presents with a central bacterial keratitis. Initial gram stain reveals gram negative rods. You decide to institute broad spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following would be the worst treatment for initial coverage:
explanation: Cefazolin has more gram-positive coverage and would be the least optimal choice. Cefazolin is a first generation cephalosporin, ceftazidime is third-generation

question: Infectious crystalline keratopathy has an unusual frosted branch appearance in corneal grafts. Which of the following organisms is most commonly associated with infectious crystalline keratopathy after corneal transplant?
explanation: Infectious crystalline keratopathy (ICK) is characterized by white, branching stromal deposits resembling snowflakes with no or minimal inflammatory signs (e.g. redness, pain). The classic scenario is a patient who has undergone a penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) and is therefore taking chronic topical corticosteroids. The most commonly involved organism is Streptococcus viridans (an alpha-hemolytic Strep species) although other organisms can also cause this entity. Treatment initially consists of topical vancomycin, cessation of corticosteroids, and possible broad spectrum systemic antibiotic use. Cases resistant to treatment may eventually require a repeat PKP.

question: What is the most common cause of infectious crystalline keratopathy?
explanation: Infectious crystalline keratopathy (ICK) is classically characterized by white, crystalline, opacities within the stroma with a relative paucity of associated inflammatory reaction. ICK is most commonly associated with relatively low virulence alpha-hemolytic streptococcus species such as Streptococcus viridans although it can be caused by beta- hemolytic streptococcus species as well. More rarely ICK can be caused by Haemophilus species, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Candida. ICK usually occurs in corneal grafts or corneas that have been treated with chronic topical steroids.

question: You are examining a 54-year-old patient who had undergone penetrating keratoplasty in the right eye 5 years prior to presentation for a corneal scar.  On exam, you note the presence of gray-white branching, needle-like opacities within the graft adjacent to a suture track.  There is no epithelial defect and the conjunctival is white and quiet.  Which of the following organisms most classically produces this characteristic presentation?
explanation: This clinical vignettte is alluding to the condition of infectious crystalline keratopathy (ICK) which was first reported in 1983 as a non-inflammatory bacterial colonization of a corneal graft. The classic presentation is in a post-penetrating keratoplasty patient on chronic topical corticosteroids who has gray-white branching opacities with a crystalline appearance in the mid-stroma. The eye is typically quiet without stromal inflammation or conjunctival injection. This process usually occurs beneath an intact epithelium though not always. The pathogenesis of ICK is not definitely known, but the bacteria are thought to gain access to the corneal stroma via epithelial ingrowth through a suture track (or via a small epithelial defect). It is thought that the bacteria evades a host immune response by depositing a biofilm around itself or via a bacterial glycocalyx. The most common causative organism associated with ICK is Streptococcus viridans which is an alpha-hemolytic type of Streptococcus. Other less common causative organisms reported in the literature include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Mycobacterium species among many other organisms. Treatment of ICK typically begins with fortified topical antibiotics with coverage against S. viridans. Examples include fortified vancomycin or cefazolin. Most clinicians will also discontinue corticosteroids if the patient is currently using them. Extra: Disease Entity Infectious Crystalline Keratopathy (ICK) is a rare infection of the cornea that results in grey- white, branching stromal opacities in the cornea with little surrounding inflammation. It has been associated with long-term topical steroid therapy and is most commonly found in patients who have had previous penetrating keratoplasty[1].

question: Which of the following organisms is of particular concern for causing post-refractive surgery keratitis occurring greater than 10 days after the procedure?

question: Phlyctenulosis is characterized by which of the following?

explanation: Phlyctenulosis is associated with Staphylococcus aureus in developed countries and Mycobacterium tuberculosis in developing countries. It presents as limbal nodules with vessel engorgement. Phlyctenulosis is generally not associated with scarring or decreases in vision. It is thought to be due to a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to bacterial cell wall antigens. They present as small rounded nodules and are surrounded by engorged blood vessels. They typically necrose centrally and involute over the course of 2-3 weeks. A scar is left behind in limbal hlyctenulosis . question: Which of the following is the most common mode of acquiring Toxoplasma gondii?
explanation: Toxoplasmosis is caused by infection by the protozoan, Toxoplasma gondii. It is said to infect up to one-third of the world's population and is the most common cause of posterior uveitis. It is thought that the most common (~50%) mechanism of acquiring this protozoan is via ingestion of undercooked or raw meat. Toxoplasma can also be transmitted to humans via ingestion of its oocytes via exposure to cat feces, soil, or unwashed fruits and vegetables. Acute toxoplasma infections are commonly asymptomatic in pregnant women, but this organism can be transmitted transplacentally to the fetus and cause death or major morbidity (e.g. blindness, intellectual disability, seizures). Therefore, pregnant women should avoid changing cat litter or handling raw or undercooked meat.

question: A 23-year-old patient presents for a contact lens exam follow-up.  He has been wearing contacts for 2 years.  He is in extended-wear lenses and sleeps in them.  For the last 2 weeks he has had mild irritation in the right eye.  On exam, you note three, 1 mm anterior stromal infilatrates in the inferior peripheral cornea 1 mm from the limbus.  You instill fluorescein and there is no staining of the lesions. There is no conjunctival injection, corneal thinning or anterior chamber cell. Which of the following is the most proper treatment?

options.A: Prescribe a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone to be used every hour and see the patient in 2-3 days
options.B: Have the patient discontinue contact lenses. No antibiotics are necessary at this time pending serial examinations with close follow up.
options.C: Have the patient use frequent artificial tears and see the patient in about a week
options.D: Scrape and culture the cornea. Have the patient discontinue contact lenses. Prescribe a broad spectrum fluoroquinolone and see the patient the next day.

explanation: These findings are very typical of sterile infiltrates due to contact lens use. The best treatment is discontinue contact lens use until they resolve (choice B) with close follow up. At this time, the clinical picture does NOT suggest an infectious etiology, but this certainly may evolve into one quickly. The best course of action, AT THIS TIME, is to discontinue the contact lenses and arrange for close follow up. Artificial tears may be given for comfort. Topical steroids may be started if after 1-2 days of follow up, there is no evidence of infection. In general, you should have evidence of infection before starting antibiotics (choice A) - needless use of topical antibiotics will eventually breed the ophthalmic super-bug that will destroy us all in a fiery blaze of corneal ulcers. Seeing the patient after a week (choice C) is also not appropriate given that this patient represents a moderate risk of developing infectious pathology, and thus close follow up would be advisable. Scraping the cornea at this time, without evidence of clinical infection, especially in the context of intact epithelium, would not be a wise choice (answer choice D). These findings could also be consistent with Staphlococcus marginal keratitis. But the least invasive treatment would be to discontinue contact lens use. Viral Infections

question: According to the Herpetic Eye Disease study (HEDS), what is the preferred treatment for herpetic stromal keratitis?
explanation: The HEDS trial showed that topical trifluridine and topical steroids expedite resolution of stromal inflammation in herpes simplex virus (HSV) stromal keratitis. The trial also examined whether adding an additional oral agent such as acyclovir to topical trifluridine and topical steroids would be beneficial and found that adding the oral agent did not provide any additional improvement. However, long term oral antiviral prophylaxis was shown to reduce recurrences of HSV keratitis leading to the general recommendation that any patient with more than one episode of HSV keratitis should be on chronic prophylaxis. Interestingly, the HEDS trial did not examine whether topical trifluridine with topical steroids is better than oral acyclovir with topical steroids. The general consensus is that an appropriately-dosed oral antiviral along with a topical steroid is an acceptable alternative to topical trifluridine with topical steroids in patients with HSV stromal keratitis. To clarify, the antiviral agent is utilized in isolated HSV stromal keratitis to prevent epithelial keratitis while on the steroid drops.

question: What was the treatment regimen for stromal keratitis in the HEDS (Herpetic Eye Disease Study) study?

explanation: The treatment regimen for the stromal keratitis arm of the HEDS study was topical prednisolone q2 hours and topical trifluridine 4x/day. Stromal keratitis secondary to herpes simplex is mainly an autoimmune phenomenon. Therefore, the main treatment involves topical steroids. The topical antiviral was used to prevent an outbreak of epithelial keratitis. The stromal keratitis arm of the HEDS study showed that there was no benefit to adding oral acyclovir to topical prednisolone and trifluridine.

question: Which of the following statements about hsv epithelial keratitis are false:

options.A: topical antivirals should generally be stopped within 10-14 days to avoid neurotrophic keratopathy
options.B: topical corticosteroids are indicated with epithelial keratitis to reduce the incidence of stromal keratitis
options.C: it is generally a self limited disease with topical therapy only shortening the duration of symptoms
options.D: valtrex should be used with caution in HIV positive patients to avoid TTP and HUS

explanation: The treatment algorithm used in the HEDS study had all the patients with HSV epithelial keratitis on trifluridine 1% (Viroptic) 8x/day. One arm of the study then divided these patients into receiving oral acyclovir (400mg 5x/day) vs placebo. The study showed that there was no advantage to adding oral acyclovir on top of topical Viroptic. But there was no part of the HEDS study that involved treating epithelial keratitis with topical steroids! This would be like pouring gasoline on a fire. Epithelial keratitis is secondary to actively replicating HSV virus. Stromal keratitis is thought to be mainly an immune reaction. So, patients with stromal keratitis are treated with topical steroids for the immune reaction and topical antivirals to suppress a potential epithelial keratitis. But, patients with epithelial keratitis only receive topical antivirals.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents to your office with complaints of left eye pain for the past 3 days. Her slit-lamp exam OS is shown in the photo above. Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the vital dye that was used in the photo above?

question: Which of the following signs or symptoms is a hallmark of herpetic-induced uveitis?
explanation: Uveitis not due to Herpes (HSV and VZV) is typically accompanied by a decrease in pressure in contrast to the uveitis seen with Herpes, which typically has an increase in pressure. The elevation in IOP with Herpetic iridocyclitis is thought to be due to a trabeculitis which reduces aqueous outflow. Uveitis secondary to other causes releases cytokines that increase uveoscleral outflow (which decreases pressure). In addition, uveitis from other causes typically results in ciliary body hyposecretion and thus decreased IOP.

question: A 30-year-old comes in with about 1 week of injection and tearing. Her symptoms started in her right eye and then appeared in her left eye. Her slit lamp exam is shown above. What is the underlying pathophysiology of her corneal findings?

options.A: White blood cell aggregation along the endothelium with granuloma formation
options.B: Contact lens overuse related epithelial erosions
options.C: Multiple myeloma associated immune complex deposition
options.D: Immunopathologic reaction localized to the anterior stroma

explanation: This patient's history of acute ocular irritation in one eye followed by the other along with the photograph showing faint corneal opacities are classic for viral conjunctivitis followed by formation of subepithelial infiltrates. Usually associated with adenovirus, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) results in a severe follicular conjunctivitis acutely. About 1-3 weeks after acute infection, multifocal subepithelial infiltrates form throughout the cornea and are believed to be a combination of white blood cells and immune-complex deposits. These complexes can result in blurred vision when in the central visual axis and may last for months. Topical steroids may be considered to aide in resolution of visually significant subepithelial infiltrates. Contact lens overuse can cause sterile corneal infiltrates, epithelial erosions / abrasions, and corneal ulcers. This patient shows stromal infiltrates, however. Multiple myeloma associated immune complex deposition is rare as opposed to EKC which is common and multiple myeloma depositions are usually crystalline in nature. Multiple myeloma is also more common in older patients (median age about 70 years). Answer choice A refers to granulomatous "mutton fat" keratopercipitates (KP) which are seen in some forms of anterior uveitis. These occur along the endothelium and are usually located in a wedge shaped region inferiorly called Arlt's triangle as opposed to this picture showing diffuse infiltrates in the anterior stroma. "Mutton fat" KP also usually appear more dense as compared to these rather faint infiltrates.

question: A 30-year-old otherwise healthy patient comes in with about 1 week of injection and tearing. Her symptoms started in her right eye and then appeared in her left eye. Her slit lamp exam is shown above. What additional feature would be LEAST likely in this patient?
explanation: This patient's history of acute ocular irritation in one eye followed by the other along with the photograph showing faint corneal opacities are classic for viral conjunctivitis followed by formation of subepithelial infiltrates. Usually associated with adenovirus, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) results in a severe follicular conjunctivitis acutely. About 1-3 weeks after acute infection multifocal subepithelial infiltrates form throughout the cornea and are believed to be a combination of white blood cells and immune-complex deposits. These complexes can result in blurred vision when in the central visual axis and may last for months. Topical steroids may be considered to aide in resolution of visually significant subepithelial infiltrates. EKC can result in either pseudo-membranes or true membranes (the rather trivial distinction being that true membranes bleed when removed). Lympadenopathy, particularly pre-auricular, is common in EKC and can help to make the diagnosis. Numerous facial and eyelid molluscum contagiosum (plus or minus follicular conjunctivitis) in a seemingly healthy patient can be a sign of underlying AIDS. EKC with subepithelial infiltrates, however, is common and not associated with AIDS Extra:

question: Which classic adenoviral syndrome is the only one with significant corneal involvement?
explanation: The majority of adenoviral eye infections presents in one of 3 ways: Simple follicular conjunctivitis. This syndrome is self-limited and without systemic symptoms. Most patients will not even seek care for this type of adenoviral ocular infection. An epithelial keratitis can occur, but it is usually short-lived and mild. Pharyngoconjunctival fever. This is the type of adenoviral infection with prominent systemic symptoms including fever, headache, and a sore throat. Again, any corneal involvement is very mild. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC). This is the only subtype of adenoviral infection with significant corneal involvement. This syndrome is characterized by rapid bilateral involvement, preauricular adenopathy, "pseudomembranes" or true conjunctival membranes, and moderate- to-severe tearing and light sensitivity. Corneal signs can include large cornea erosions and/or multifocal subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs). These SEIs can be so prominent as to obscure vision. Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome is not an adenoviral ocular infection. Extra: Epidemic Keratoconjunctivitis - serotypes 8,19,37 Pharyngoconjunctivitis - serotype 7 Simple follicular conjunctivitis - multiple serotypes

question: Which of the following clinical findings is commonly found in epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC)?

options.B: multifocal subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) developing within 3 days of onset of symptoms
options.C: fibrin formation in the anterior chamber

explanation: There are many viruses that can cause "viral conjunctivitis" and they are broadly divided into DNA viruses and RNA viruses (see outline below). The DNA viruses more frequently result in vision-threatening forms of ocular inflammation and include adenoviruses. There are 4 classic types of conjunctivitis that are caused by different adenovirus serotypes: • Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) • Pharyngoconjunctival fever (PCF) • Acute nonspecific follicular conjunctivitis • Chronic keratoconjunctivitis The causes are: simple follicular conjunctivitis (multiple serotypes), pharyngoconjunctival fever (most commonly serotype 3 or 7), and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC; usually serotype 8, 19, or 37, and subgroup D). Clinically, the syndromes are indistinguishable in the early period. Adenoviral follicular conjunctivitis is not associated with systemic symptoms. Pharyngoconjunctival fever is associated with flu-like symptoms: fever, pharyngitis, and preauricular adenopathy. Adenoviral follicular conjunctivitis and pharyngoconjunctival fever generally don't have epithelial keratitis. EKC causes the most severe form of adenoviral conjunctivitis. 7-10 days after inoculation, patients develop a severe follicular conjunctivitis and punctate keratitis. The conjunctival inflammation ranges from mild inflammation and a mixed follicular/papillary reaction to a severe reaction with subconjunctival hemorrhage, true and pseudomembranes. Keratitis (i.e. corneal inflammation) does not always occur in EKC, but if it does, can be classified into stages: • Stage 0: minute punctate opacities within the corneal epithelium (barely perceptible); within ~2 days of onset. • Stage 1: more easily-observed punctate epithelial keratitis (both with and without fluorescein staining). • Stage 2: coalescence of these lesions and involvement of the deep epithelium ("coarse PEK"). • Stage 3: faint subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs) appear beneath the coarse PEK; typically during 2nd week. • Stage 4: "classic SEIs" (i.e. very easily-observed, multifocal SEIs); typically during 3rd week. • Stage 5: "punctate epithelial granularity" adjacent to and distinct from the SEIs Patients develop multifocal subepithelial infiltrates about 7-14 days after ocular symptoms start. Therapy is supportive and steroids should only be used if there is vision threatening subepi infiltrates or conjunctival membranes. Steroids can prolong the course of the disease and some patients may need them permanently once started. NSAIDs don't help the subepi infiltrates. Patients are considered infectious if they are still hyperemic and tearing. • DNA viruses commonly causing conjunctivitis o Adenovirus o Herpes simplex virus o Varicella-zoster virus o Epstein-Barr virus o Cytomegalovirus o Variola and vaccinia virus o Molluscum contagiosum virus • RNA viruses commonly causing conjunctivitis o Picornaviruses o Paramyxoviruses o Togaviruses o Flaviviruses

options.C: epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC; usually serotype 8, 19, or 37, subgroup D)

question: Which of the following is an effective treatment for adenoviral conjunctivitis:

options.A: use of topical NSAID for subepithelial infiltrates
options.C: removal of membranes by forceps to prevent entropion
options.D: use of steroid prophylactically before there are any corneal changes to prevent central corneal opacity

explanation: Steroids should, in general, never be used with infectious processes. They should not be used routinely with adenoviral infections. They may be used in select cases where opacification of the central cornea is occuring. NSAIDs have not proven effective for the treatment of subepithelial infiltrates. Other measures that help with adenoviral conjunctivitis include artificial tears and cool compresses, removal of membranes by forceps to prevent entropion, and use of steroid to prevent central corneal opacity (but never prophylactically).

question: Which of the following is a recommended treatment for a patient presenting with recent-onset, herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO)?

options.A: acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day for 14-21 days if the patient is immunocompetent
options.B: trifluridine eyedrops 9x/day until resolution of a pseudodendrite
options.C: topical amitriptyline to prevent post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN)
options.D: intravenous acyclovir if the patient is immunocompromised

explanation: The term "herpes zoster ophthalmicus" (HZO) is typically reserved for varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (i.e. CN V1). Patients with HZO present characteristically with vesicular lesions involving the upper eyelid and forehead area. These patients may initially complain of a prodrome of fever, malaise, and warmth and a vague uncomfortable sensation in the affected dermatome. According to the BCSC, ocular involvement occurs in >70% of HZO patients and inflammation can occur within any ocular tissue. Some examples of characteristic ocular findings in HZO include: • Conjunctival injection (e.g. papillary or follicular reaction) • Pseudomembrane formation, conjunctival scarring • Episcleritis, anterior or posterior scleritis • punctate epithelial keratitis, pseudodendrites, anterior stromal infiltrates • neurotrophic keratopathy (typically later) • keratitis, endotheliitis • anterior/posterior uveitis • sectoral iris atrophy Management of the acute manifestations of HZO typically includes: 1. Systemic antiviral therapy. For non-immunocompromised patients, the typical regimen is oral valacyclovir 1 gram tid OR acyclovir 800 mg 5x/day OR famciclovir 500 mg tid for a 7-10 day course. Systemic antivirals have been demonstrated to reduce viral shedding from the skin lesions, reduce the chance of systemic dissemination of the virus, and decrease the incidence and severity of the ocular complications. In addition, if begun within 72 hours of the onset of symptoms, systemic antivirals may also decrease the duration of any postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) that occurs later. However, systemic antivirals have not been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of PHN from developing. 2. Any ocular inflammation is treated with topical steroids and cycloplegics. Topical antivirals are typically NOT used for ocular involvement in HZO. 3. The skin lesions are typically treated with a topical antibiotic ointment (e.g. erythromycin) to prevent a bacterial skin superinfection. Warm moist compresses are used for comfort. 4. For immunocompromised patients, intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg q8hr) is administered to prevent these patients from developing disseminated disease (e.g. encephalitis). 5. Oral steroids are sometimes used by some physicians to help with early zoster pain. However, their use remains controversial at this time. Most acute zoster pain can be treated adequately with oral analgesics. The main overall morbidity from herpes zoster is due to post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) which is commonly defined as the skin pain or dysethesia that occurs >30 days from the date of onset of the attack. The management for PHN is beyond the scope of this question, but some typical therapies include: oral gabapentin (brand: Neurontin), pregabalin (brand: Lyrica), amitriptyline, and capsaicin cream. Answer choice "A" is wrong since the recommended duration of oral antivirals is typically 7-10 days. Answer choice "B" is incorrect since topical antivirals are not typically used for ocular involvement in HZO. Answer choice "C" is incorrect since oral (not topical) amitriptyline may be associated with a decreased duration of PHN if given early in the course of disease and continued until pain symptoms remit. Other notes: The ophthalmic division (i.e. CN V1) further divides into the nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal branches. It is actually the frontal branch that is most commonly involved in herpes zoster infections. However, involvement of the nasociliary branch confers a higher risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the extensive innervations of the nasociliary nerve with the eye (e.g. conjunctiva, sclera, cornea, iris, and choroid). The lacrimal branch is least commonly affected by HZV. As you probably know, "Hutchinson's sign" describes when vesicles are present on the side of the tip of the nose. This sign indicates infection of the nasociliary nerve and thus a higher likelihood of ocular involvement by HZV. Extra:

question: Which of the following branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (i.e. CN V1) is most commonly involved in herpes zoster infections?
explanation: There are three divisions of the trigeminal nerve: ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular. The ophthalmic division is most commonly affected in herpes zoster infection of the trigeminal nerve. The ophthalmic division (i.e. CN V1) further divides into the nasociliary, frontal, and lacrimal branches. It is actually the frontal branch that is most commonly involved in herpes zoster infections. However, involvement of the nasociliary branch confers a higher risk of ocular involvement. This is due to the extensive innervations of the nasociliary nerve with the eye (e.g. conjunctiva, sclera, cornea, iris, and choroid). The lacrimal branch is least commonly affected by HZV. As you probably know, "Hutchinson's sign" describes when vesicles are present on the side of the tip of the nose. This sign indicates infection of the nasociliary nerve and thus a higher likelihood of ocular involvement by HZV. question: A 10-year-old child presents with a red eye for the previous four months. On your exam, you note a follicular conjunctivitis. He also has the skin lesions seen in the photo above. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this child's presentation?
explanation: These 1-2 mm "umbilicated", dome-shaped, skin-colored papules are classic for molluscum contagiosum which is caused by a DNA poxvirus called "molluscum contagiosum virus" (MCV). MCV is spread via direct contact with infected individuals. Typically, these nodules involve the eyelid margin, but occasionally can be found on the conjunctiva itself. MCV is one of the common causes of chronic follicular conjunctivitis and is thought to be caused by shedding of virus particles from the eyelid (or conjunctival) nodule. Other causes of chronic follicular conjunctivitis include: inclusion conjunctivitis (Chlamydia), trachoma (Chlamydia), and toxic follicular conjunctivitis (e.g. glaucoma drops, antiviral drops). Spontaneous resolution can occur, but is oftentimes prolonged on the order of months to years. Faster recovery can be achieved by excision of the offending lesions, cryotherapy, or incision of the central portion of the lesion. One last high-yield pearl is that extensive molluscum lesions should prompt a workup for HIV infection

question: A 10-year-old child presents with a red eye for the previous four months. On your exam, you note a follicular conjunctivitis. He also has the skin lesions seen in the photo above.  Which of the following is the best treatment option for this child:
Which of the following is the most common manifestation of Congenital Rubella Syndrome:
explanation: The systemic manifestations of CRS are deafness (most common systemic sign), cardiac malformations (e.g. patent ductus arteriosus), and ocular findings. Of the possible ocular findings, pigmentary retinopathy is the most common in CRS. Despite the striking appearance of the fundus, vision is not typically affected by this pigmentary retinopathy. Instead, poor vision in CRS is usually caused by cataract and microphthalmos. The classic teaching is that cataract and glaucoma do not occur simultaneously in CRS. The most common cause of poor vision in children with CRS are cataract and microphthalmos. Extra:

question: A prostitute brings her 10-year-old son to be examined by you in the office.  He has been experiencing difficulty seeing and eye irritation.  On exam he has mulberry molars and a saddle nose.  You examine his right eye first and notice interstitial keratitis and "salmon patch" vascularization.  What is the chance that he will have involvement of the left eye as well?
explanation: Syphilitic interstitial keratitis (IK) typically presents late in the first decade of life and represents an immune-mediated manifestation of congenital syphilis. Other nonocular signs of congenital syphilis include: • dental deformitis (e.g. notched incisors and "mulberry molars") • saddle nose, saber shins, frontal bossing, perforation of the palate • deafness • mental retardation Congenital syphilitic IK usually presents bilaterally in 80% of cases although there may be asymmetry in the degree to which each eye is affected. The typical clinical progression of this disease entity is: • Initial symptoms of pain, tearing, photophobia, and perilimbal injection • Sectoral superior stromal inflammation and keratic precipitates seen early • Deep stromal neovascularization occurs later. This stromal vascularization can be intense enough to turn the cornea pink ("salmon patch"). • Inflammation spreads centrally and corneal opacification and edema develop • Corneal scarring and thinning with ghost vessels

question: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (AHC) is characterized by which of the following:

options.B: commonly caused by coxsackievirus A24 variant

explanation: Acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (AHC) can have follicular conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhages. It is commonly caused by enterovirus type 70, and coxsckievirus A24 variant. It is rarely caused by adenovirus type 11. There is no such thing as EgC virus. Neoplastic Disorders

question: You see a patient in clinic with a pigmented conjunctival lesion.  You do an excisional biopsy and the results come back with the diagnosis of conjunctival melanoma.  Which of the following factors does not worsen the prognosis?
explanation: Conjunctival nevi generally present in the first or second decade of life. Limbal nevi tend to be flat while nevi of the bulbar conjunctiva, plica semilunaris, and caruncle tend to be raised. The color can vary from light brown to amelanotic. Approximately 50% contain epithelial inclusion cysts. Observation is generally recommended. Excision should be considered if growth occurs. Benign nevi are rarely found on the palpebral conjunctiva. Therefore, these lesions should always be biopsied if they are found on the palpebral conjunctiva, tarsal conjunctiva, the caruncle, plica semilunaris, or in the fornix. Complexion-associated melanosis (also called racial melanosis or benign acquired melanosis (BAM)) is more associated with persons of darker complexions. It presents with pigmented patches more noticeable near the limbus. It generally is generally bilateral and fairly symmetrical and occurs in adulthood. Primary acquired melanosis (PAM) is generally unilateral and highly asymmetric. It is generally non-cystic. It most often occurs in light-skinned individuals in middle age. Factors that increase risk of progression include: more than 3 clock hours of conjunctival pigmentation, or those involving the caruncle, fornix, or palpebral conjunctiva. Involvement of more than 2 clock hours is an indication for removal. Cellular atypia is the most important factor for predicting progression. PAM without atypia rarely turns malignant and can be followed every 6-12 months. PAM with mild atypia should be monitored more closely. PAM with moderate to severe atypia has a high risk of progression and every effort should be made to remove the entire pigmented conjunctival lesion. If the lesion is too large for removal, topical Mmitomycin C can be used. Conjunctival melanoma generally occurs in middle to late adulthood. It is often nodular and vascular. The overall mortality rate is 25%. They are most commonly found in the bulbar conjunctiva or limbus. About 25% are amelanotic. The origin of melanoma is from PAM (70%), nevus (5%), and de novo (25%). Conjunctival melanomas have a greater than 50% rate of recurrence. Factors that portend a poor prognosis include: • location in the palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle, eyelid margin, or fornix • invasion into deeper tissues • thickness greater than 1.8 mm • pagetoid or full-thickness intraepithelial spread • lymphatic invasion • mixed cell type • de novo origin (i.e. not starting out as PAM or nevus) • tumors not involving the limbus • residual involvement at the surgical margin Excisions of pigmented lesions should include a 2 mm uninvolved margin and avoidance of touching the pigmented area of the lesion when handling to prevent seeding (i.e. "no touch" technique). Incisional biopsies should be avoided because they can spread tumor cells.
